speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
May I, in the absence through illness of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, make on his behalf an announcement concerning a Canadian aid program in southeast Asia. The announcement is being made simultaneously elsewhere.
For a number of years the United Nations commission for Asia and the Far East has been conducting a series of investigations and studies of the development possibilities of the lower Mekong river basin. The Mekong is one of the great rivers of the world. Its total length is about 2,600 miles, and its length in the lower basin is 1,600 miles. It actually rises in southern China but for most of its course it flows through or between
Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and South Viet Nam. The economic health and the political stability and independence of these countries are in large measure related to this great river.
The development of the lower Mekong offers great economic benefits to the four riparian states and, indeed, to the region as a whole, in terms of flood control, irrigation, hydroelectric power and improved navigation. The realization of these benefits, however, is still many years away. Some preliminary planning and survey work has been done but further progress cannot be made without first obtaining more reliable and detailed data on the basin. The development possibilities are so encouraging that the United States, New Zealand, France, Japan and several agencies of the United Nations have already contributed men and resources to carry out these further investigations.
For our own part, while the bulk of Canada's aid under the Colombo plan has been and should be concentrated in commonwealth countries, the government considered that this project was sufficiently challenging and promised such great benefits as to warrant some Canadian participation in it. Moreover, the government was influenced by the fact that these benefits would go in substantial degree to countries with which Canada has been closely associated in recent years through our membership in the international supervisory commissions in Indochina.
We therefore made available the services of Lieutenant Colonel G. S. Andrews, surveyor general of the department of lands and forests of the province of British Columbia, to make a detailed study of the problems and estimated costs involved in the aerial surveying and mapping of the Mekong river which, as hon. members will appreciate, is an essential first step toward the eventual realization of the potential benefits of this project.
On the basis of Colonel Andrews' report the Canadian government has now decided to participate in the first priority phase of the survey and mapping of the main stem of the Mekong river. This work, which Canadian companies are particularly well qualified to undertake, is expected to extend over two years and will involve an aggregate Canadian contribution of up to $1.3 million. It is the intention of the government to finance

Announced Canadian Aid to Southeast Asia this contribution from Colombo plan funds which parliament will be asked to appropriate in 1959-60 and 1960-61.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had an announcement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding supplementary action in the matter of assistance to a particular underdeveloped country, and now the Minister of Finance on behalf of his colleague makes an announcement regarding assistance to a development project along the Mekong river which extends through Indo-China and, of course, through part of China itself.
The little country of Laos, with which Canada has had association through the international truce commission, based on the agreements of 1954 and concluded at Geneva, will receive assistance from Canada. The agreements are now to be given further emphasis by this additional assistance amounting to $1.3 million, which is part of our Colombo plan project. I am not aware from what the minister said whether this assistance will extend to the neighbouring country of Cambodia or to the larger neighbouring country of Viet Nam.

and social problems of underdeveloped countries, and in this instance in Asia.
We do this, I take it, as was always done before, without any conditions attached. We do this because we feel that at this difficult time in the history of the world those nations that are more fortunate than others must in accordance with capacity share in the building up of the standard of life of those countries, and in this way we make our contribution to the easing of international tension in our time.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT CONCERNING IMPOSITION OF TOLLS  TABLING OF NOTES

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT CONCERNING IMPOSITION OF TOLLS  TABLING OF NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
make a statement regarding the agreement reached between Canada and the United States on the tolls to be charged on the St. Lawrence seaway. With the concurrence of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I now table copies in English and in French of the exchange of notes dated March 9, 1959, constituting an agreement between the Canadian and United States governments. The agreement makes provision for the division of the toll revenue, for the method of collection, for future minor amendments of the tariff and for the constitution of a joint tolls advisory board to hear complaints with respect to interpretation of the tariff or alleged unjust discrimination.
The tariff becomes effective from April 1, 1959. The whole concept of defraying the cost of construction and maintenance of the seaway, including the cost of deepening and maintaining the Welland canal as an integral part of the seaway by charging tolls, was provided for in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act of 1951. This principle was fully debated at that time and passed without dissent by parliament.
The tariff of tolls agreed to has the same rates recommended by the tolls committees of the seaway entities on June 12, 1958. Some changes and clarifications have been made in the definitions of bulk and general cargoes.

Statement on St. Lawrence Seaway Tolls
The tariff of tolls is based on a composite assessment which encompasses a charge per ton of cargo actually carried together with a charge per gross registered ton of the vessel, and will be applicable to all vessels whether laden, partially laden or in ballast.
The method of assessing and collecting the tolls and rates was adopted with the following objectives: one, procedural simplicity which will minimize the cost of collection and expedite the dispatching of vessels; two, recovery of the cost of the seaway and its operation on a basis which will provide economic rates to users and encourage traffic.
The rates will be as follows: 1. A vessel will be assessed 6 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 42 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 95 cents per ton of general cargo carried. 2. A vessel will be assessed 4 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 40 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 90 cents per ton of general cargo carried. For partial transit of the new seaway facilities between Montreal and lake Ontario, where there are seven locks, the user will be charged for each lock transited 15 per cent of the toll for complete passage.
3.	For each passage through the Welland canal only a vessel will be assessed 2 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 2 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 5 cents per ton of general cargo carried. In the Welland canal a partial transit will be assessed 50 per cent of the toll for complete passage irrespective of the number of locks used.
Other main features of the agreement and tariff of tolls are: First of all, commercial vessels carrying passengers will be charged 50 cents per passenger for each lock transited between Montreal and lake Erie, in addition to the vessel and cargo charge. The charge for a complete transit of the seaway will be $7.50 per passenger. The tariff will apply to all types of craft using the seaway, including government owned or government operated vessels except vessels of or employed by the seaway entities. Pleasure craft will be subject to the same rates as other vessels except that there is a minimum charge for pleasure craft of $2 per lock transited. The minimum charge for all other vessels will be $4 per lock transited.
The unit of weight for the collection of tolls will be a ton of 2,000 pounds. Provision is made for prior registration of vessels and satisfactory security to be given for the payment of charges subsequent to which passage will be permitted. Toll collection and invoicing of accounts, as well as the preparation of statistical data, are assigned to the St. Lawrence seaway authority at Cornwall. The
66968-9-118
St. Lawrence seaway development corporation will participate in the billing and collecting operation and will share in the annual cost of these services. Charges will be billed to the ship owner or representative promptly and will be payable within 14 days of the date of billing. An additional charge for non-payment within this period may be levied in an amount not to exceed 5 per cent of the amount due.
For through passages to or from Montreal and lake Ontario the invoice will show two amounts to be paid; 1, Canadian funds to cover the portion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway authority of Canada, which has been intially set at 71 per cent of the total charges, and 2, the balance of the account, or 29 per cent, in United States funds representing the portion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation. Tolls for passage on the Welland canal will be paid in Canadian funds only.
Bulk cargo as defined in the tariff of tolls includes such goods as are loose or in mass and generally must be shovelled, pumped, blown, scooped or forked in the handling and, without limiting the generality of the term or otherwise affecting its meaning, it is deemed to include barley, buckwheat, corn, dried beans, dried peas, flaxseed, rapeseed and other seeds, flour, grain screenings, mill feed containing not more than 35 per cent of ingredients other than grain or grain products, oats, rye and wheat, loose or in sacks; cement, loose or in sacks; coke and petroleum coke, loose or in sacks; domestic package freight; liquids carried in ships' tanks; ores and minerals, loose or in sacks, including alumina, bauxite, coke, gravel, phosphate rock, sand, stone and sulphur; pig iron, scrap iron and scrap steel; pulpwood, poles and logs, loose or bundled; raw sugar, loose or in sacks; and wood pulp, loose or in bales. All commodities not included in the definition of "bulk" are classified as general cargo.
The agreement provides that the toll revenue for that portion of the seaway between Montreal and lake Ontario be shared proportionately to the annual charges of the two seaway entities. The agreement also permits, under appropriate procedure, changes in the list of goods defined as bulk cargo.
The joint tolls advisory board to be constituted will consist of four persons, two of whom shall be appointed by the St. Lawrence seaway authority and two by the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation. The board will hear complaints relating to the interpretation of the tariff by the authority or the corporation, or with respect to alleged unjust discrimination arising out of the

Statement on St. Lawrence Seaway Tolls operation of the tariff, and report its findings and recommendations to the authority and the corporation.
The two seaway entities are charged with the duty of reporting to their respective governments not later than July 1, 1964 as to the sufficiency of the authorized tolls to meet the statutory requirements and to cause the tariff to be reviewed accordingly. Reviews of the tariff at other times may, of course, take place by decision of the two governments.
As hon. members know, this great inland waterway will become operative with the opening of the navigation season this year, and we have every reason to look forward to a material increase in the volume of shipping using these facilities. This should be of great assistance to the development of the commerce of this country as a whole, and should enable goods produced in Canada to become more competitive in world markets. We look forward to the whole economy of Canada benefiting with the opening of this great seaway project.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
For a
moment, Mr. Speaker, I thought I was listening, particularly during the last part of the minister's remarks, to a speech made by myself. However, I am sure the house will welcome the statement the minister has made, because it will give notice to shippers and ship operators of the tariffs which the two corporations intend to charge in ample time for them to get ready for the opening, which we hope will bring that voluminous amount of traffic which the minister and others have stated.
There are two questions which came to my mind while listening to the statement. The minister stated there would be established a joint tolls advisory board, composed of two representatives from Canada and two representatives from the United States, to deal with the tariff of tolls. My first question is this. The minister will remember that last year when he made a similar announcement prior to the tolls being investigated by the two groups, I asked him whether the board of transport commissioners would have jurisdiction over these tolls. He replied that they would, in conformity with a section in the St. Lawrence seaway authority statute. My question is, why has this change been made?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT CONCERNING IMPOSITION OF TOLLS  TABLING OF NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the whole house has listened with great interest to this very important statement. However, I think everyone
[Mr. Hees.l

realizes that it takes time to digest a lengthy statement like this, and particularly the attached documents. I am not one who is given to making off the cuff endorsations or condemnations until I have had an opportunity of studying the situation. This represents the view of this group. We are unable to assess fully, from the information received, the impact of this agreement on the various sections of Canada or on certain industries, agricultural producers and so on. We will therefore have to reserve our objective and informed comments until a later date.
However, this is a two-party agreement, completed between the governments of Canada and the United States. We realize that in those circumstances we cannot have all we want if we are to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement. We do hope the government has done its very best in securing this agreement to protect the interests of all sections of Canada. We all know, I think, that the government has received representations from certain provincial governments in Canada, and possibly from some sections of industry, urging a toll free St. Lawrence seaway. I was pleased to note, while listening to the minister's statement, that there is provision in the agreement for consideration of complaints by persons concerned to the board authority. I do hope they take every advantage of that provision in the agreement to bring to the attention of the government the views of various industries, producers and users of the canal across Canada with the idea that as time proceeds the arrangements under this agreement will be satisfactory to all sections of the Canadian people.
In conclusion I want to mention that these requests which have come from various provinces and certain industries and producers in Canada for free tolls spring from the increasing costs of transportation in Canada at this time; that is their basis. I think the protests and the whole argument in support of free tolls are convincing evidence of the necessity of the establishment of a national transportation policy in Canada at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT CONCERNING IMPOSITION OF TOLLS  TABLING OF NOTES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Laurier, the answer to his question is that the joint advisory committee has been established because it is considered by the St. Lawrence seaway authority, the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation and the governments of the two countries that this will be the most efficient and fairest method of dealing with representations and complaints, if any arise, from shippers and other interested parties.

I should like to raise one other matter. It has to do with our general attitude toward Indians, which I hope will change as we progress. Generally we in Canada look with abhorrence upon racial discrimination which exists in other parts of the world. We decry the attitude that exists in certain sections of the United States toward its negro population. We view with distaste the approach of apartheid in certain parts of the world such as Africa. Generally we pride ourselves on being free from discrimination in Canadaj and we say that other countries certainly are not as far advanced in racial equality as we are.
I do not think we should pride ourselves too much on that, because there still exists in a number of places in Canada, consciously or otherwise, an attitude of discrimination against native Canadian peoples in terms of providing them with employment and accommodation in hotels and things of that nature. I know we cannot legislate, though we have tried it in some provinces in Canada, to make that type of discrimination illegal, because it is an attitude of mind on the part of one group as against another. I only express the hope that in the future we shall think more in terms of an attitude of equality toward our native Indian people, far more so than we have done in the past.
I should like to deal with one other specific item. Inasmuch as we shall be establishing a joint committee of this house and the other place shortly-at least I hope it will be shortly-there will be ample opportunity to go in the fullest possible detail into the problems of our native Indian peoples, and I hope we shall find some solutions to them. Therefore my remarks will be rather general and brief on this occasion.
There is a question affecting our native Indian peoples, namely the question of liquor as it relates to the native Indian, that I should like to deal with. On March 4 there was a news item in the Vancouver Province which apparently arose out of a letter that a Mr. Andy Pauli from Vancouver had sent to the minister, asking that native Indians there be given the right to buy liquor in liquor stores and also packaged goods-they are called that-in liquor stores and take them home. The announcement of the attorney general of British Columbia was to the effect that the first move, in so far as liquor rights for Indians were concerned, was entirely up to the Indians themselves.
I suppose in the strict and narrow sense, without taking into account the full provisions of the Indian Act in so far as liquor

is concerned, the attorney general was correct. But I think someone should either bring him up to date on what the law of this country is, or he should go back to law school for a little while to find out what is in the Indian Act; because the attitude of the attorney general in that province is not conducive to providing equality of opportunity for our native Indian peoples.
He says that in the first instance it is up to the Indians themselves. I would point out the ridiculous situation which would exist if Indian band councils were to take advantage of a section of the Indian Act having to do with the right to have liquor on the Indian reserves without having the right to be in possession of liquor in other parts of the province. An Indian band council could do this under a section of the Indian Act. If they took that action and the attorney general of British Columbia, or the attorney general of any other province, did not object within 60 days; if they had a referendum and the reserve decided that they wanted the right to consume liquor on the reserve, we would find that they would be in the ridiculous position of having the right to consume liquor on the reserve but no right to buy it or to keep it there. They would have the right to drink in a beer parlour, as they have in British Columbia, but they could not buy a case of beer in a beer parlour and take it home on the reserve, where they could have the right to have it if they were to follow the suggestion of the attorney general.
So far as British Columbia and the other provinces are concerned, the matter rests squarely on the shoulders of the provincial governments from the point of view of taking the initiative. Certainly Indian band councils could take the initiative but, as I am sure the minister realizes, that would merely promote a chaotic situation.
Our liquor laws as they relate to Indians are a bit foolish. We hear the comment that Indian people cannot handle their liquor, that they do all sorts of wild things when they have access to liquor, and therefore we should not allow them to have it or, if we do, only under strict conditions. It is quite true that when a native Indian gets a little too much of the corn under his belt he becomes drunk, obnoxious, loud-mouthed, sloppy, argumentative and wants to fight. It is quite true that is what happens to the native Indian; in fact he is almost as bad as the white man who does the same thing. There is no difference.
I should like to point out the ridiculousness of our liquor laws as they apply to native Indians. Depending on who and 66968-9-119

In the past Frank Calder, by reason of the position he then held as a member of the legislature, was invited to a number of receptions. He was an Indian, a member of a band and prohibited from drinking liquor, but he was invited to a number of receptions and he went. The R.C.M.P. were there and they did not interfere in any way. Yet Frank Calder broke the law respecting liquor rights as much as it was possible to break the law. I do not blame him one bit; I would do the same thing myself if I were in his position. Again, not only at the reception I have mentioned but at every session of the provincial legislature Frank Calder was invited to a reception by the lieutenant governor of the province.
There is another awkward relationship involving a native Indian and the liquor laws. It has to do with a gentleman who is a member of the other place. Because of his background, because of his race, because of the position he holds, no doubt he has been invited to many receptions in the past at which liquor was served and undoubtedly he will be invited to similar receptions in the future. As the situation stands now, having regard to the province of Ontario only, if that hon. gentleman as a member of the other house accepts an invitation to such a reception he is in order. He is not contravening the law.

Furthermore, all references concerning various guests whom the lieutenant governors of the various provinces may wish to have at their receptions are quite out of order. Furthermore, we cannot refer in this house to actions of lieutenant governors or matters affecting provincial legislatures.

Mr. Chairman, if I may raise a point of order, I quite agree with and I am not protesting what Your Honour has said about lieutenant governors and the Governor General, but surely when because of his race the hon. member for Skeena referred to a person who happens to be in the other place he was simply illustrating a point with respect to Indians, and was not discussing that gentleman's conduct in the other place or any speech he has made or anything he has done as a member of the other place. He was discussing the fact that an Indian was a member of the other place and was subject to additional embarrassment for that reason. It seems to me that it would be very restrictive indeed to our liberties in discussing the administration of the Indian Act if Your Honour were to insist upon so narrow an interpretation.
The government is very touchy on this subject.

As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, it is not my intention to embarrass anyone but merely to attempt to show the foolishness of our liquor laws as they apply to some people in Canada. However, I can say that a few years ago I deliberately invited a native Indian into my home, an Indian who was a member of a band and prohibited by law from consuming liquor in any other place except a licensed beer parlour or cocktail bar. Incidentally, Indians cannot get into the cocktail bars because of the discriminatory attitude of their operators. I invited this Indian into my home and offered him a drink. I mentioned to the R.C.M.P. beforehand what I was going to do and I was told not to worry, that they would not do anything about it. That again shows the ridiculousness of our liquor legislation. All I am trying to point at this time is that the situation is screwy, and that some action should be taken immediately.
You were trying to get someone into trouble.

I was trying, my friend says, to get somebody in trouble; that is about the extent of his knowledge of this situation. I am here to point out the necessity for an attitude of equality toward the people of this country whether their skins be coloured the same as yours or differently; whether they happen to have been born of parents who were in this country many years before my parents were in this country, or under any other circumstance.
I point out that our attitude toward these people is not one of equality but one of discrimination. This is another phase of it, and the problem rests squarely on the shoulders of the province. I know the Indian Act has been amended, in effect, to remove as much as possible the jurisdiction of the minister with regard to the liquor question as it relates to Indians. This problem has been pushed where it belongs, under the jurisdiction of the various provincial governments. I am complaining that they are at fault in not working in the direction in which they should be working. There is one province, Ontario, which is far advanced in so far as the question of liquor is concerned, and I wish to heaven the other provinces would follow suit.

I was glad, Mr. Chairman, last week to hear the minister say that it is the government's intention to see that the Indian population receive greater consideration. I understand that the department

of Indian affairs is conducting an experimental program in Manitoba which has to do with the rehabilitation of Indians who have been disabled by tuberculosis. This is a very commendable beginning, but it should not be limited to Manitoba. We have similar cases in the district of Thunder bay. It seems to me that Indians who have spent several months or years in a sanatorium should be helped, no matter where they live.
I suggest that Fort William or Port Arthur could be considered as an ideal centre for the establishment of a rehabilitation centre in one of the lakehead hospitals, preferably in one of the wings of the Fort William district sanatorium. Young men and women could be trained as orderlies or nurses' aides. These Indians could be taught some trades to enable them to become useful citizens, and at the same time give them a feeling that they are part of the community and enjoying equality of treatment, which I believe should be the answer for all Indian problems.
Another great need is adequate recreational facilities. The problem of unemployment is greater for the Indians than for the rest of the population because of their isolation. This makes constructive recreational outlets doubly important, as the young people tend to drift around and get into trouble. A few years ago, as a result of the generosity of the president of Canadian National Railways and a few people in Fort William, a small building was made available for recreational purposes. This has helped to some extent. However, the lack of proper direction and adequate assistance has limited its usefulness. Here is a place where the government can really do something which would not cost a great deal.
It is rather regrettable, but the Indians still do not have the full benefit of all the services provided by the Ontario government that other people enjoy. An example of this may be found in the matter of mothers' allowances. I submit that while the public welfare authorities may be experiencing certain difficulties in extending their services to Indians, and while a certain amount of time will be required to achieve a smoothly functioning procedure, this should not prevent them from receiving the full benefit of all our welfare services.
At the present time when an Indian family is destitute the amount of assistance it receives from the department is much below that which would be required for even a minimum standard of subsistence. If the act were amended so that a reserve would be regarded as a municipality for such welfare purposes, with the department of Indian affairs assuming the responsibility together with the band and the province providing its usual 66968-9-1194

During a recent visit to my constituency I attended a meeting of the local Indian band, which is the Ojibway tribe. Their chief, Frank Pelletier, welcomed me to their reservation school and outlined some of their needs and grievances. He felt that there was a need for higher education. He deplored the neglect in the past, but hoped that the coming generation might obtain an education which would enable the Indian to stand on his own feet in a competitive world.
The next most important need is housing. The Indians do not have the funds to decently house their growing population. Some houses which were constructed a few years ago were poorly built; they were too low; they sagged, and the doors and windows stuck. Here, surely, was a case of total indifference and a definite lack of good workmanship. They do not ask for ultra-modern buildings, but something good and solid.
These Indians certainly complained about not having a vote in federal elections. This indeed seems to be a paradox. They can vote for a provincial member but they are not allowed to vote for a federal member when, in reality, it is the federal government which has jurisdiction over their affairs.
The majority of the men are employed cutting pulpwood, but their limits are almost exhausted and within two or three years this source of livelihood will be gone unless the government provides some new limits. There are several islands in the district with good stands of timber which would be ideal for their purpose. Some time ago some individual from the department of Indian affairs made a survey, but nothing has been heard of the outcome. There seems to be a lack of co-operation, if not total neglect, on the part of the department of Indian affairs in Ottawa.
In so far as education is concerned, the elementary schools are well conducted and presided over by competent teachers. One of them, Mrs. Mary Duggan, attended the meeting. She made the suggestion that in order to prepare pupils to absorb a higher education they should be given some vocational training, such as carpentry for the boys and sewing for the girls. The department should look into the matter, since it would not cost much to set up a couple of rooms in the basement of one of the schools and have someone supervise at least a limited vocational training program.
All the pupils capable of absorbing education wishing to attend high school in the city should be provided with transportation. A small bus or even a station wagon would

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration probably meet the requirements of those on the reservation. One father whose family lives in the reserve at Squaw bay, which is approximately seven miles from the nearest high school, has three children who wish to go to high school, but there is no means of transportation. That is just a case in point. Some 12 children do attend high school in the city, and they walk two miles to the nearest city bus line. Road conditions within the reservation are also poor and this matter came in for a lot of criticism from the gathering. Only $6,000 had been appropriated for road work in three reservations, which means that only a bit of patchwork on each can be expected.
The Fort William reservations own mount MacKay, which is about 900 feet above the level of lake Superior, at the back of which the Fort William watershed is located. That is a lake known as loch Lomond, which is seven miles long and about half a mile wide, from which lake our city gets its water. I might add that it is the purest water on the continent, flowing by gravity through a tunnel on the mountainside and piped to the city. It is so pure that it needs no distilling for any purpose. The purity and taste of this water have been favourably compared with the water flowing from the summit of mount Ben Nevis, which is the highest peak in the British isles, in Fort William, Scotland. There is a road leading up around the ledge of the mountain some 600 feet high, at the end of which there is a chapel and also a cross erected in memory of the Indian soldiers who fought and died in the first great war. This side of the mountain could be beautified, and with a good road would become one of the major tourist attractions of the lakehead. I believe the department should look into this feature as a means of revenue for the Indians of the local reserve.
Another question which is worthy of consideration is the status of the Indian in relation to our liquor laws. Our Indians are asking for the same privileges enjoyed by other people. It is rather a shame that an honest, civilized human being, because he is one of the original Canadians, upon entering a beverage room is faced with a large sign which reads, "Anyone caught serving an Indian will be prosecuted". Such is not the treatment that the forebears of our present Indians were promised when they all too trustingly agreed to let the white man take over most of their possessions. How can we speak of bills of rights when we are condoning such an injustice? In the event of war these men would be in the armed services. Many of them have served with distinction in both world wars, yet they are faced with the worst type of discrimination. Let us have

equal privileges for equal responsibilities. This glorious country of Canada cannot and should not have two classes of citizens. To quote the Indian chief of our tribe himself at this particular meeting, he said:
There is good and bad among all classes of men, but the majority of my people are law abiding and should be recognized as such.
Now I wish to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail in late February of 1959 and which contains a few paragraphs of an address delivered by Professor W. J. Morris of the University of Toronto:
Across the country, he said, Indians constitute the most economically depressed segment of our population. A once proud and noble people showed a high degree of co-operation toward the encroaching whites; and as their inheritance they are "tossed from municipal to provincial to dominion governments like the proverbial football".
He recalls that for decades there was a pitiful lack of educational facilities on reserves, and those that existed were furnished by the churches. These and welfare conditions have improved, but Indians forced off the reserves "by threat of starvation" find no comparable services among whites. For our 111,000 Eskimo, said Professor Morris, we spend more than twice as much as we do for 173,000 Indians. "This in itself is second class citizenship." And we need only recall recent testimony of Eskimo hardship to visualize the lot of the Indians.
With "our first real Indian act" dating only from 1951, Professor Morris says we have "operated on a hit and miss basis": and among his suggestions is research both economic and in the area of inter-personal relations, together with inter-government co-operation at all levels to utilize voluntary resources. "We have for long enough refused to accept any measure of responsibility as individuals for what is in effect the sorest blight on our Canadian conscience."
Those are important words. Two centuries of official bungling and evasion of a great human problem are in the last analysis a reproach on the monumental indifference of the Canadian people. It will in turn be their pressure which will give Indians their rightful heritage of first class citizenship.
As a matter of fact, the press of the country appears to be unanimous in its estimate of the situation. After 200 years since the royal proclamation, which said that no Indian could be dispossessed of his land without the crown's consent, this charter signed in 1763 being a guarantee of equality, these promises have not been fulfilled according to its terms.
I have a copy of another editorial which appeared in the Calgary Herald, which further illustrates, if more illustrations are needed, that the plight of the Indian is a question which concerns all Canadians. I quote:
Canadians are quick to offer advice and gratuitous opinions on racial problems in other countries. Yet Canadians are part of what might be called an unintentional conspiracy to keep the Indians as second class citizens. Canada's record with the native Indian population has some items of merit

to its credit over the years. Unfortunately we have only to look at the Indian population to realize that an entirely new approach is needed, and should be speeded to suit modern conditions.
Mr. Chairman, this is undoubtedly an accurate appraisal of the present status of our Indian population. I do not wish to cast any aspersions, or blame this or any former government. I simply express a belief and desire on the part of the great majority of the Canadian people that the time has arrived for the government of Canada to translate good intentions into a practical reality. I respectfully submit that the question of helping our Indian population is an urgent one and should be dealt with during this session of parliament.

First of all, may I say that I am wondering why the hon. member for Skeena spent so much of his time dealing with the question of liquor for Indians. I think the big problem which faces the Indian today is the opportunity to earn enough money to make a living so that in the long run he may have enough money left to buy his liquor after he gets his permit.
With regard to what he said about the difficulty experienced by an hon. member in the other place, I personally think that the hon. senator should apply for enfranchisement if he wants to drink liquor. All he needs to do under the terms of the Indian Act is to apply for enfranchisement.
I wish to express my appreciation today for the consideration which the minister has given to the question of destitute rations and to the problem of housing. In past years, as the hon. lady knows, I have been very critical of the meagre rations distributed to Indians who are destitute or who have returned to their homes from tuberculosis hospitals after being cured of T.B. The minister has given us the details with regard to destitute rations, and I wonder if she would be good enough, when she replies, to give us similar details with regard to rehabilitation rations, in particular those rations which are given to people who have returned from tuberculosis hospitals.
In each of the past five years the amount set aside in the estimates for providing Indians with housing, at least in my part of the country, has increased. However, I do not think it has increased at the rate it should have increased if we really intend to impress upon the Indians that we are conscientiously and seriously concerned about their living standards. I think we could well increase a great deal more those estimates, particularly where they concern the Northwest Territories.
I was happy to see that some attention has been paid to the economic development of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration native Indians. If I understood correctly the minister's statement the other day, it was to the effect that a new division would be established within her department in order to deal with the economic aspect of the development of our Indian people. I am wondering, however, if this new division will have any jurisdiction in the Northwest Territories, and I say this because I heard recently that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has carried out a reorganization of their department and have set up a new division in that department known as the welfare division. I understood the minister of northern affairs to say that this new division in his department would look after not only the welfare of Eskimos, as it has done for many years, but also the welfare of Indians, white people and all others in the Northwest Territories.
I notice also that a new section of the department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was set up this year, namely the industrial section. This section involves, I imagine, a duplication of what the department of Indian affairs has done in setting up its new economic development section. I hope the minister will be able to clear up this matter when she replies, and say whether her department will have jurisdiction with regard to the welfare and economic development of Indians in the Northwest Territories or whether this work will be the responsibility of the department of northern affairs.
I wish also at this time to express my appreciation of the very fine work done by the officers of the hon. lady's department in my riding. In recent years we have found these officers coming into my riding in greater numbers, and we are thankful for that, and I am confident they are all very interested in the native people and anxious to bring about changes which would make it possible for Indians to realize a standard of living which could be compared, at least to some extent, with our own. I should like to make a suggestion to the minister with regard to the economic development of our Indian people.
As the minister knows, we have Indian agencies in the Northwest Territories at Yellowknife, at Smith, in Norman and Akla-vik, Hay River and Simpson. Each of these agents has to cover a very large area if they are to get into close contact with the natives and understand the problems of the communities over which they have jurisdiction. I wish to suggest to the minister that
the department should hire works foremen_____
let us call them that-in every settlement in the Northwest Territories where there is an Indian population. The duty of these work foremen would be to guide and give leadership to the Indian people in their economic

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration development. The people appointed should be men who know the conditions in the north, people who have lived in these communities, not someone who has just come out of the University of Toronto with a degree in welfare. The people I have in mind should be practical men who have lived with the Indians and who are interested in doing something to improve their conditions.
A further suggestion I have to make concerns co-operation between the Indians and the works foreman. I think any Indian agent would agree that in my part of the country, at least, the co-operation of the Indian chief of each particular band and settlement is very necessary if the government hopes to "sell" to the Indians a policy designed to raise their living standards and help them advance from their present static condition. The co-operation of the chiefs is very necessary in most cases if the government is to be successful in bringing the Indians out of the depths of poverty. I understand that in some parts of Canada the chiefs have not the same influence over their tribes as they had many years ago. But in the Northwest Territories they still have great influence over their people, and I suggest to the minister that her department should pay the chiefs some sort of salary for working in co-operation with the works foremen to which I have referred and helping to convince his people of the benefits of government policy in the field of economic development.
I also think that in every community there should be provided a tractor with a blade, a sawmill and a powered scow. I will go into this matter in somewhat more detail, pointing out what I think each of these pieces of equipment will or can do in order to help the Indian to place himself in a position where he can at least make a living like any other person in Canada.
At this time I would like to deal with the Great Slave lake area in particular. There are many communities centred around this lake including Yellowknife, Rae, Hay River, Fort Resolution, Rocher River and Snowdrift. Great Slave lake is considered to be the world's greatest source of whitefish and trout but on this lake you see only a handful of Indians working in the industry of commercial fishing. In my opinion many more of these people could be employed in this industry but you cannot say to an Indian, "Here you have this lake; the fish buyers are here so go out and fish." Any commercial fisherman must have a considerable amount of equipment. I suggest to the department that it should set up some sort of loan fund for Indians all around the lake including those people at Fort Providence and Fort Simpson who every fall go up the Mackenzie river into the lake to do their domestic fishing under


which a loan plan could be established. In other words these people could borrow money to equip themselves under the guidance of the works foreman to whom I previously made reference and establish themselves in the profitable business of commercial fishing on Great Slave lake.
Another thing that would be of assistance would be to have the department request the Department of Fisheries to conduct surveys to investigate the various inland lakes such as Lac la Marte to establish whether or not they are suitable for commercial fishing. If, for instance, Lac la Marte was found to be suitable for this purpose a number of our Indian people in the area around Rae, Lac la Marte and Hislop lake could be profitably employed in commercial fishing. I urge the department to take some steps toward supplying these people with guidance and equipment to encourage them to become engaged in useful projects of this type.
A few moments ago I said that every settlement in the district should be supplied with a tractor and other equipment. I appreciate that the first question that will be asked is: What will the Indians do with this equipment? In the Northwest Territories we have vocational training schools. Here the Indians are trained as operators of tractors and other equipment. These trained operators could be used during the early winter before the snow became too deep in hauling out logs cut by other Indians in the bush to supply the people in the area with material for proper housing for themselves. At the present time they tend to construct clapboard or plywood homes under a contract basis. I believe the Indians should be encouraged to haul out their own logs from the bush and build suitable homes for themselves.
The sawmill could square the logs and it could be operated by our native people under direction and guidance. There is no reason why one or two Indians from each settlement could not be trained in sawmill work at the vocational schools.
I also urge that a powered scow be provided at each settlement. Any person who has lived among Indians or dealt with them is aware that when winter comes they are faced with the problem of heating their homes. These people usually live for today with no real thought for tomorrow or the future and so their homes are heated from day to day as it were. If a scow were provided it could mean that those Indians who were unable to obtain salaried employment during the summer months could work in the bush cutting wood and transporting it to the settlements to provide themselves with a supply of firewood for the winter, and also

they could sell wood to those Indians who were gainfully employed on a payroll.
There are other things that could be done. Possibly some land clearing equipment could be provided in areas where there is land suitable for growing vegetables. The men could work the equipment and the women could look after the seeding and weeding and assist with the crops.
At this point I cannot resist telling the committee about a trip I took down the Mackenzie river in 1954 with the then minister of northern affairs and national resources. It was his first trip north after his appointment and of course at every place we visited the civil servants shined up the brass and showed us all the nice things in the north. We eventually arrived at Fort McPherson and were given a wonderful dinner. When we left the dining room the local school teacher invited the minister, the deputy minister and others including myself to see the garden project. We discovered six or seven Indian women pulling weeds in the garden. By the time we arrived there only half the garden had been weeded. The word had gone around that the minister was coming and the garden should be cleaned up quickly and although they had started at it in the morning they had not completed it by the time we arrived. If we had arrived in the morning before the warning had gone out we would have seen nothing but weeds in the garden.
There are, however, Indians in the north who have initiative and who are interested in working. They tell me that garden projects of this kind operated on a community basis is for the birds. They explained that some of them work very hard all summer in the garden and when the fall comes the crop is taken off and shared with the whole community. They said they would rather see the government split up these garden plots into individual acreage. They prefer to work their own plots and take off the produce that is the fruit of their individual labour.
That was a C.C.F. policy.

An hon. member comments that communal gardens were a C.C.F. policy and I agree. I have explained what has been happening under that policy. I hope the department will change its tune on that score and give these people some opportunity for individualism, a goal to work for and a degree of personal initiative.
I have dealt with some of the things we could do to improve the lot of the Indian people. It must be pointed out, however, that the fur industry is still the backbone of the economy of the native people in the Northwest

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Territories. In the past several years fur prices have been so low that in many places it is not worth trapping fur. I appeal to the minister and ask her to see her friend, the Minister of Agriculture, and ask him why we cannot bring fur under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Everything else that is produced in this country can come under the act. The raspberry growers, the pulpwood cutters, grain grown in eastern Canada, and just about everything that is grown comes under the act. Sheep come under the act. Wool of the sheep comes under the act. Everything from soup to nuts comes under the act. The minister told me last year that even the fur ranchers in Canada who ranch mink and other furs come under this act, but wild fur cannot come under it. I appeal to the minister and I am sure that with her sweet smile she can convince her colleague the Minister of Agriculture that wild fur should come under the act. If she cannot do that, then I would suggest that the department of Indian affairs should start to look at the proposition of putting a floor price under furs, covered by separate legislation, if we have to.
In the past four or five years there have been-and I am sure the director, or any of the officials of the department will agree with this-a number of Indians employed in construction projects at Inuvik, at Fort Smith, at Yellowknife on the road, and so on. The minister mentioned this as a matter of fact in her statement. This year we are in the process of moving the town of Aklavik to its new location. At Fort Smith we are building government houses for civil servants and offices for civil servants. Most of the building that is going on is for civil servants and some Indians are working on those projects. Those construction programs will be over and finished in two years. Ever since we started that construction program I have repeatedly said that we had to look to the future. It is fine and dandy to have Indians on the payroll today and making a half decent living, but the minute that construction is over what are you going to do with the Indian? This is the problem and now is the time to start thinking about it. What are you going to do with the children who are coming out of the vocational training schools that we have built in all parts of the country. This is a problem that requires serious consideration now.
I noticed the minister said we will have placement officers. Have we one in the Northwest Territories? If we have, has any thought been given to what the placement officer is going to do to place Indians if there is nothing for them to do? How are we to encourage native children to take vocational training two or three years from now when their older brothers and sisters have come

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration out of school and are back on the trap line trapping muskrats because there is nothing else for them to do? This is a serious problem. If we do not do some planning now we shall force the native Indians four or five years from now to reject the whole basis of education and he will have reason to do so. He goes into a school and takes a course as a grader operator, an electrician or any sort of operator but when he comes out of school the construction work is finished and he has no job. Then the government asks him to go back on a trap line, something he has never done before. He does not know how to trap; he is useless as far as trapping is concerned. If we do not do some serious thinking now this will happen.
There is an immediate solution at least for those who have been trained in the last few years and for those who are being trained right now. I would suggest that the Department of Transport be notified of every native who is a mechanic or who is able to operate a piece of equipment such as a snow blower, a grader, a tractor and the like, all of which are required, as the committee knows, for the maintenance of airports, with the view of filling all the vacancies from now on with natives who have been through the vocational training courses provided by the government and who I am sure can handle any piece of equipment that is sitting on any airport in the Northwest Territories.
This, I say, is something we should do immediately. We should provide every department of government operating in the country with a list of qualified people whom they might require for their work. I suggest also that before the construction season opens this year the contractors who have been successful in getting contracts at Inuvik, Fort Smith, Hay River, Fort Simpson, Yellowknife, and on all the roads that are going north, be supplied with a similar list. It should be made plain to them that native people are to be employed before they start shipping in carloads of people from the outside. The Northwest Territories has the highest percentage of unemployment in Canada, regardless of what anyone says. When native people who have been told, "you take a vocational training course and you will receive jobs", find themselves out of work during the construction season and find, as I said a moment ago, carloads and aeroplane loads of men being shipped into the north to do jobs they could do, how do you think they feel about it?
I would also suggest that we provide a list to the Imperial Oil company down in Norman Wells and to the transportation companies, both the crown-owned Northern Transportation Company and the Yellowknife Transport, and ask for their co-operation.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter coming under this vote upon which I should like to make a few comments. It is one which has not been discussed so far and I admit that it is somewhat complicated. Nonetheless, I hope that the minister will be able to give the committee some information about it. May I say first of all that I am raising this matter at the request of the president of the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood.
We all recognize that property and civil rights and natural resources come within the jurisdiction of the provinces while Indian affairs come within the jurisdiction of the federal government. However, it has been mentioned to me on a number of occasions and again recently by the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood that they would like to have a clear exposition from the minister as to how far she feels her responsibility extends in the conduct and direction of Indian affairs having regard to ownership of property and Indian rights within the boundaries of provinces, particularly where no treaty rights are involved.
We all recognize that the minister is faced with problems right now involving the Six Nations Indians and it may be on a somewhat similar basis that I have been asked to raise this matter in the committee at this time. I have been told on many occasions by Indian chiefs in British Columbia that they have never given over their ownership of British Columbia because there is no treaty under which they did so. However, I am not going into that phase of the matter this afternoon.
May I say that I am quite proud that the native Indians of British Columbia should take such interest in whether or not they hold ownership to lands and certain rights in respect of timber or minerals. In recent years they have expressed great interest in the development of the province and great interest particularly in the last year as to who will develop the province. They are primarily interested in the northern part of British Columbia where, as the minister knows, approximately one-fifth of the territory of British Columbia apparently is to be ceded by the Social Credit government of our province to a corporation or group of corporations nominally headed by Axel Wenner-Gren but behind whom we know are the Krupp interests of Germany. The Indians are concerned as to their status in the development of that part of the province under that type of ownership. I believe that the Indians of British Columbia generally

and the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood are to be congratulated, complimented and commended because of their interest in this matter. Perhaps the best way I can present the matter to the minister and the officers of her department is by doing what I was requested to do by the president of the grand council. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I will read the letter I received under date of February 20 on the official letterhead of the brotherhood. It reads in part as follows:
By the provision of section 109 of the B.N.A. Act, the title to the minerals and soil in a province is in the crown, the province and the Indians. Lord Watson in giving judgment for the privy council in the St. Catharines Milling case ruled in part as folows: "There is a third interest, and that interest is the Indian interest, which is capable of being vindicated in competition with the provincial interest."
By that fact and by law, as fortified by the privy council judgment. .. the B.C. Indians have an interest equal to the province but wacky Bennett has not consulted us in giving a big portion of what belongs to us Indians to Axel Wenner-Gren. The reason for this letter is to ask you to speak for us in the House of Commons and ask what kind of a man is this Axel Wenner-Gren? Is he worthy of a man to be allowed into British Columbia? The people of B.C. who are co-owners of what Bennett is going to give him... from the grapevine and the moccasin telegraph this Indian has been told by white people that Wenner-Gren made his millions dealing with human lives.
I say that that statement, Mr. Chairman, is a correct one. I continue:
That during world war II he dealt with the enemy, while also doing business with the allies.
That too is a correct statement, Mr. Chairman. I continue:
Is this gangster, who is worse than Capone, the kind of a man to do business with? What comes after this donation by Bennett may be detrimental to all the people in B.C. We may be enslaved, we must protect our posterity.
This comes from the Indian brotherhood in the interests of British Columbia, their own land. The letter continues:
You can use my name in these allegations because as the chosen leader of my people it is my duty to know and can only find this out through your questions in the parliament of Canada. The query must be directed to all hon. members of the House of Commons, not only the government, because they are the trustees for the Indians of Canada-The land that he is to get is rich in minerals, etc., and will adversely affect the economy of the Indians in that part.
I was asked to raise the matter in the house. That is signed by Andy Pauli, grand chief and president of the North American Indian brotherhood.
I felt it was my responsibility, Mr. Chairman, having received the letter to read it. As I previously stated, it is something to be proud of that our truly native-born Canadian citizens, our native Indians, are concerned
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration about the development of our natural resources, and who develop them. Basically their question is, what power, what influence, what interest has the minister in charge of Indian affairs at this time, to assist them in a situation in which British Columbia is making a deal with a man who, by order in council, was declared a traitor and a person with whom no one could deal during the last war.
I was so interested in the letter and in the other statements made that I checked on the St. Catharines Milling and Lumber Company case, a decision of the privy council, which is to be found in Canadian Constitutional Decisions of the Judicial Committee by Olmsted. I am not going to go into the decision in detail, but I did find some interesting facts in that judgment of the privy council. May I just give a couple of quotations which I feel are important. On page 238, the judgment says:
Documentary evidence was referred to, to show the nature and character of the Indian title. It was contended that the effect of it was to show that from the earliest times the Indians had, and were always recognized as having, a complete proprietary interest, limited by an imperfect power of alienation.
On page 241, we find this:
It is contrary to the spirit of the act to hold that the grant of legislative power-
That is the British North America Act.
-over lands reserved for the Indians carries with it by implication a grant of proprietary right.
I am not going to continue with that, but I do believe sincerely that the North American Indian brotherhood has raised a most interesting, if complicated, question. I do hope that the minister may find it possible, because of her interest in the department over which she exercises jurisdiction, to take note of the situation in British Columbia and the interest of the native Indians of British Columbia in their own proprietary right to develop the resources of the province, who develops them, and perhaps inform the native brotherhood through the medium of what she says in this house as to what their position is and what help they can expect in defending, not only their own hunting and fishing grounds but the natural resources, thereby honouring their ancestors who were the original settlers of that great province.

I have two or three questions to ask the minister which I have been directed to ask by some people in Ottawa. Are there any solicitors employed by the department in connection with Indian affairs? If so, what are their salaries and have they passed the necessary examinations to qualify as solicitors in any province of Canada?

There are a few questions I should like to put to the minister before she replies. I do not intend to make a speech, and I am sure she will be relieved to hear that. I think we would all be interested in the most up to date information she has about what is going on on the Six Nations reserve. It did happen, I think it was last night or at any rate very recently, that I was looking at television which I do not very often do. I saw the superintendent of the Six Nations reserve on television. He expressed the view- I am not taking any exception to this or anything of that sort-that the sooner we found out what the people of that reserve really wanted, the better.
As a matter of fact, this had already occurred to me even before I saw this television program. I thought perhaps it would be advisable-I am only putting this forward very tentatively because I think the minister appreciates I have no desire to make any difficulties at all in connection with this matter-to have a plebiscite on the reserve to ascertain whether or not the majority of the Indians want to continue to have an elective council or want to have the restoration of the government of the so-called hereditary chiefs. I know there would be considerable difficulties if the second course happened to be the wish of the people because of the claims that are made by the hereditary chiefs that they are not Canadian citizens and the reserve is not a part of Canada but an independent country.
I have to confess that I do not know whether or not this course has ever been taken or ever been considered. It may be that at one time a decision was made by the courts on this matter. I understand that there was a certain treaty in the time of Sir Frederick Haldimand which had a good deal to do with the status of the reserve and of the Indians living on the reserve. I am wondering if possibly it might be a good idea, by agreement if agreement can be secured, to refer that document and any of the other relevant documents to the supreme court, with a view to getting an authoritative interpretation of them. I imagine there would not be much purpose to be served in doing that unless there was a prior agreement with the parties interested that they would accept an interpretation by the supreme court. It might be impossible to obtain such an agreement.
These two ideas had crossed my mind, and I thought, it would be useful to put them forward. I do not expect the hon. lady to make any particular comment about them. However, I would appreciate it, and I think other members of the committee would, in


view of some of the things that have been happening, if without taking too much time we could be told as much as the hon. lady has in the way of information as to what is occurring.
I am also very much interested in being brought up to date, as I am sure would be other hon. members of the committee, about the progress of the famous expropriations at Caughnawaga. I have spent a good deal of time on, and given a good deal of attention to, this subject, and I am sure the hon. lady has done the same and I would again like to know what the current situation is. While I am not seeking to go underground or anything like that, I would also like to hear a little more about water mains and the sewers, and how they are coming along at Caughnawaga.

I told you all I knew
the other day.
I was hoping in the meantime the hon. lady had instructed herself a little more.

I thought I gave a pretty
full answer, but I will see if there is any more information.

I would be very much
interested as well, although perhaps the hon. lady would rather do it at a later stage, but I will ask the question now, to hear how the scholarship scheme has worked out and to have a brief report on that. I think I can say, with my usual modesty, that I had something to do with starting that scheme, and one is naturally interested in the things one starts oneself. I would also be quite interested in knowing what the experience has been with what I think was the last thing I had anything to do with starting in the Indian affairs branch, and that was the provision of relief in cash instead of in kind. I know I had some little difficulty in persuading some of my colleagues on treasury board that some Indians on selected reserves should be treated like other people with respect to relief, and it was agreed it would only be an experiment. I think it was one of the steps in the right direction which I would like to see taken as fast as people will agree to them and circumstances permit. I am sure the hon. lady will, without even being asked, tell us what the latest progress has been in the integration of the schools; that is to say, in getting Indian children into schools attended by other children in the various provinces.
There may be some other questions which will occur to me later on, but they are the ones which occur to me now.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to ask the minister a question about a matter which has arisen on the Indian reserve at Gleichen. The situation there is one of concern as regards the financial difficulty of the Indians on that reserve. A situation has arisen whereby the Indians, who for a number of years have farmed their own land and built up a capital reserve, now find that that capital reserve has diminished and that they are in such financial difficulty that they are unable to farm their own land. Also, consideration is being given to renting that land to the white man. This is a sort of reflection on the administration of that Indian reserve, either through the failure to have farm management men there to assist and supervise the Indians in the proper management of their land, or it could be due to a number of other causes. Nevertheless, the fact remains that the Indians on that reserve now find it necessary to seek jobs off the reserve in order to gain a livelihood. It seems to me that the Indian affairs branch should, in their wisdom and administration of the affairs of that reserve, give careful consideration, if they have not already done so, to the step which is now contemplated.
That land belongs to the Indians, and I submit that before it is leased to the white man and before long term contracts and commitments are made, the Indians' fundamental problems should be probed to the very depths in order to see if by financial help or other arrangement something cannot be done by this government to bring about a situation on that reserve where these Indians can profitably administer and farm their own land.

I wonder if I might briefly pose a couple of questions to the minister. I understand that we make a grant to the national commission on the Indian Canadians. I would like to know how much that is. I cannot find any reference to it in the details, but it is the amount of the grant we make which I want.
You will find it under the citizenship branch.
Is it listed as an amount?
No, it is not. I will find it for you.

Thank you. My other question is this. On October 30 and 31, 1958 there was a provincial conference of Saskatchewan Indian chiefs and councillors held at Fort Qu'Appelle. I would like to take the liberty, if I may, of reading one of the resolutions passed at that conference. One reads:
We, the chiefs and councillors of the association of Saskatchewan Indians, in conference assembled,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration request the federal government to undertake a detailed social survey of Saskatchewan Indians to among other things
(1)	gather factual information on the conditions prevailing on all reservations;
(2)	make recommendations as to policies and programs designed to provide for the advancement and improvement of Saskatchewan Indians, and
(3)	determine the most effective methods of implementing these programs.
I wonder if the minister would indicate whether the association of Indian chiefs has officially communicated the contents of this resolution, or the import of it, to the minister, and what action has been taken or is contemplated with respect to the suggestions made therein?

Mr. Chairman, possibly I could try to answer now some of the questions which have been put in the course of this debate. In so doing, may I thank the hon. members for their interest and say to them that all of the constructive suggestions which have been made will certainly be dealt with by this department, and consideration will be given to them. There are two or three very good suggestions which have come out of the debate today. I might say further that the officials of my department are ready and willing at all times to consult with members who wish to bring to them suggestions, or who wish clarification of existing conditions on any of the reserves.
With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena, perhaps I should answer his last reference first. The resolution from the conference at Fort Qu'Appelle was forwarded to the branch and we have it. There are certain difficulties in the way of proceeding immediately; the matter is under consideration. I might tell him that it took five years from the time of the first consideration of the report now known as the Hawthorn report on the British Columbia Indians before the study was finally undertaken. These things cannot be done overnight. If my memory serves me well it is now something in the nature of two years since the suggestion was first made that a similar study, or something approximating the same kind of study, be made amongst the Indians in Saskatchewan. We are considering the matter. It is the opinion of those who have studied the Hawthorn report that much of the material in that report is of general interest to Indians right across Canada, and we do not wish to duplicate the work which was put into that report. I can assure the hon. member that the matter is under study at the present time. Eventually there will be a study made, but that will depend upon the speed with which we can arrive at terms of reference establishing such a study.

I noted what the hon. member had to say with reference to relief payments. I am sure he will agree with me that the schedule now established represents a great improvement over that formerly in effect. I cannot let this opportunity pass without commenting on the fact that last year when this subject was under discussion I maintained, from the available figures, that the average relief payment made was around $14. The hon. member maintained it was $10, and the press of this country picked up that amount and made it known that the amount of relief payments to Indians was $10, despite the fact that I had given a different figure. This year, however, when payments have been increased to a minimum of $22 for the first single adult, the hon. member indicates that this represents a very small increase. comes under provincial jurisdiction. However, even before it becomes a matter of provincial jurisdiction the Indians themselves must make their wishes known to the provincial government which in turn makes a request to the federal authorities. Thus I imagine that the statement by the cabinet minister in British Columbia which he read would have reference to the fact that the initiative must come from the Indians if they wish to have the liquor laws changed with regard to the consumption of liquor on the reserves.
Does this provision that the initiative must rest with the Indians themselves form part of the Indian Act?
No. The request must come from the province, but the province naturally does not move until it is sure of what the Indians want.

Since the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has returned, perhaps I might deal with some of the matters he raised. I should like to refer first of all to the situation at the Six Nations reserves. Possibly I had better tell the house what has already become public knowledge since it happened last night after the house rose.
Yesterday on the Six Nations reserve the new Iroquois police, as they style themselves, arrested one of our school teachers, an Indian by the name of George Beaver. They charged him with treason because he had written a letter to a local newspaper criticizing the action of the hereditary chiefs. They incarcerated him in the basement of the council house where they kept him for some time. They finally tried him for treason. I understand they found him guilty and then released him with a warning not to do it again. However, Mr. Chairman, it is my opinion that we must protect Canadian citizens and accordingly I should like to read into the record the telegram which I sent to Joseph Logan, Sr. who has been speaking for the hereditary chiefs. It reads as follows:
Joseph Logan, Esq.,
Ohsweken,
Ontario.
It has been brought to my attention that citizens have been molested and detained by an alleged Indian police force on the Six Nations reserve said to be under the direction of your organization. I am further informed that some of these persons have been subjected to mock trials and in some instances ordered to pay fines.
This type of conduct cannot be tolerated and I must most emphatically advise all those members of the Six Nations participating in and who are responsible for such unlawful conduct that it must cease immediately.
I must further inform you that steps will be taken without delay to restore and maintain peace and order on the Six Nations reserve for the protection and quiet enjoyment of all citizens.
The telegram is signed by the minister. I am not sure whether the hon. member made a suggestion or was thinking out loud, but with respect to his remarks about the proposed plebiscite I may say that is something that has occurred to some of the members of my staff. We have been discussing the matter. I think little would be achieved by proceeding in the heat of the present situation but I draw to his attention also that in any event nothing can be done at the moment because the authority of the hereditary chiefs is being argued at the present


time before the courts in Ontario. Until that matter is settled I think we would be wrong in taking any action.

I wonder whether the hon. lady would allow me to interrupt her for the purpose of obtaining information. How did that case get there? I do not want to say anything about the case but how did it get before the courts? Is my memory failing or is it something that occurred since the hon. lady became minister?

I think it was already started when I came into the department. As I understand the situation, and my officials will correct me if I am wrong, the hereditary chiefs challenged the action of the elected council with regard to the sale of a piece of property.
That would have been after my time.

The matter is now before the courts and, of course, we must await the outcome. The hon. member also asked me a question with reference to Caughnawaga. The area expropriated was 1,374.14 acres.
