The total amount of compensation paid to individuals as of February 24, 1959, was $2,217,892.20.
Have any of these cases gone into the courts?

No, there are none in the courts. I said in the absence of the hon. gentleman that I thought that the rest of his questions had to do with education. Would he like to wait until we reach the education item?

I would be quite happy to wait until that time. However, another question has been put to me. Perhaps it is a little unfair of me to ask the hon. lady without trying to find out for myself but as she has so much more research staff than I have perhaps she will not mind. It has been represented to me by some Caughnawaga Indians that they are very fearful of this proposed metropolitan Montreal arrangement. They feel Mr. Duplessis is attacking the autonomy of the Caughnawaga reserve. I wonder if the hon. lady knows whether the reserve is to be included in the metropolitan area or definitely excluded?
I can assure the hon. gentleman I have made no changes in the law. As he knows, under the present situation no one can encroach on a reserve, so the Indians are quite safe.

It occurred to me it would, of course, be quite incompetent for the provincial legislature to attempt to legislate a reserve into part of a municipality. I did not think there could be anything in this, but I thought there would not be any harm in asking the question since it had been put to me.
No, not at all. As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me well, we did have some correspondence with at least some members of the band in that regard, and gave them that answer.

There is another question about Caughnawaga, and that is the question of re-routing the road and re-routing the bridge. Have all problems of that sort been settled with the provincial authorities and with the Indians?

I do not know that they have been settled. The Indians have objected to any change in the road and so long as their objection stands nothing will be done about it. Unless they can come to an agreement, nothing will be done. I believe that some of the provincial authorities wanted to discuss the matter with them, but they were not even amenable to that suggestion so the department does not intend to take any action on the matter so long as the opinion of the Indians is that they want no change.
There were also some expropriations at St. Regis. Have they all been settled?
The area of the reserve expropriated was 140.3 acres; the number of individuals entitled to compensation, 40. All of the settlements have been completed and the total compensation paid was $184,771.
Well, that is a happy ending.

I have one very minor question before this item passes. It relates not only to this particular vote, but to every other vote in the book. At the last session I urged that something be done about this, and if I could indicate it to the minister now perhaps she could communicate with the authorities responsible for the compilation of the statistical information in the estimates book. What I am suggesting is this: in the second portion of the book containing the details of the services, would it not be possible to arrange to print in that section the number of the vote, just as it is in the front of the book? We find great difficulty in following exactly what vote we are dealing with in the detailed section.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I wondered if I raised the question at this session, perhaps next session and eventually we will be able to have the vote number printed in the detailed sections of the book.
If the hon. member will mention it to the Minister of Finance when his estimates are before the committee, he will be putting it to the proper authority.
Will the hon. lady join me?
I shall be glad to.

The hon. lady will remember that there was a good deal of debate and a good deal of agitation at one time about the completion of the band lists, particularly in relation to certain happenings in Alberta that were ultimately settled in the courts, as they should have been in the first place. There were, the last time I made inquiries, still a few cases pending and I just wondered if the hon. lady could bring us up to date, and let us know if that job is also completed?
It is practically completed, Mr. Chairman. The protests remaining are down to two, and we hope that these will be handled to their satisfaction shortly.
Are these two persons living on the reserve or not living on the reserve? I would be interested in their history. Perhaps I could find a grievance.
The reason they have not been settled is that we cannot locate them.

This is an old favourite of mine, as the minister well knows. Perhaps the minister would like to leave this until we resume at eight o'clock, when she could tell us just where these estates stand. It is one of the most vexing problems, as I found when I was in the department, and I am sure a lot of us hope the situation is improving steadily. I should like to have a fairly detailed report on what the situation is.

I think with all the information I have at hand I can manage to give it to the committee before six o'clock. The estates which were concluded in 1956-57 were 1,420; in 1957-58, 1,179; 1958-59-this is just from April to December-the last figure I have is 2,412. Now, in the management of estates opened, in the 1956-57 year we find they were 667; in 1957-58, 702; and in 1958-59, for the same period April to December 31, 508.
Has the hon. lady the global figure for the backlog at present?
My officials do not have the figures for the backlog at present.
I think there are a couple of other questions I should like to ask, so perhaps we could let this stand.
From the information I gave, the hon. member will realize we are cutting steadily into the backlog.
I think it is very encouraging.

How far we have gone, I could not say at the moment, but I shall try to find out.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We have been discussing item No. 59. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to address a few remarks on the first item before it carries. There are a number of items which are of some concern to the Indian people of the Yukon. I want particularly to draw to the hon. minister's attention matters concerning housing, children's aid, welfare payments in isolated areas, education, both schools and hostels, and land. Perhaps I could first refer to the minutes of a meeting held in Whitehorse between the


superintendent of the Yukon agency and five members of the legislative council of the Yukon, as well as Commissioner Collins. At that meeting the main topic of discussion was the matter of welfare payments to Indian people in isolated areas. The following resolution was passed:
Be it resolved, in order that the economic welfare of Old Crow, Ross river and such other areas as may be found necessary at a later date, be better secured, it is desirable to pay to each adult Indian or person living the Indian mode of life, who kills a wolf by means other than poisoning and delivers the pelt to the R.C.M.P., the sum of twenty dollars as a rehabilitation measure for an experimental period of not more than three years. The pelt to remain the property of the person killing the animal.
This matter of welfare I have already discussed with the director of the branch, who has been very helpful and who has given me reason to believe that some sympathy, perhaps, exists in the branch for the people of these rather remote areas, and that they may expect some assistance in this regard.
Another subject which was discussed at this same meeting was the matter of the allotment of land. I would like to call to the attention of the minister the fact that the five members of the legislative council of the Yukon were present at this meeting and all these resolutions were passed unanimously, with the exception of the one concerning the re-establishment of the bounty, and that received unanimous consent with the exception of one voice. This resolution concerning land was passed:
Be it resolved that inasmuch as no treaty exists between the Indians of the Yukon, and the government of Canada, it would seem desirable, with the consent of the Indians of the Yukon, to make some arrangements regarding individual and band land allotments at this time as a measure of security.
This matter of the allotment of land to the Indian people of the Yukon is one which should be of some concern to the minister, as I am sure it is. The time has come when some arrangement has to be made for the Indian people of the Yukon. If it is not the intention of the department to allot tracts of land, which was the normal course followed in other parts of Canada, may I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to setting up band council funds in lieu thereof.
The territorial council at its last session considered these matters, and I have before me a copy of the votes and proceedings of the legislative council which was prepared last year. In debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, Councillor George Shaw of Dawson said this:
Another matter, Mr. Speaker, that I feel strongly about, is the matter of extermination of predatory

animals, more specifically the wolf. I can quite understand how nature balances the continuity of the different species of animals; however, I do not think that nature always takes into account, in its balancing, the effect that man has created in his need of game animals, either for meat or sport. Accordingly, statistics have proven that caribou are very much decreasing in number; the people who feel the impact of this most severely are the Indian population that subsist primarily on these animals for food and clothing, etc. To assist these people, whose very lives depend on these large herds continuing, I consider it imperative that a bounty be placed on wolves. Such an action without question will substantially deplete the wolves in the area concerned; also will assist the Indian trappers in what is now a most depressed industry.
These remarks of Councillor Shaw may be used to point out the present need for consideration being given to the resolution which was passed at the meeting of December 29, 1958, at Whitehorse. Councillor Shaw brought up another matter at the last session of the legislative council when he discussed the education of young Indian people. In this same debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, he says:
It is commendable, and I welcome the government's plan, to provide vocational training to the younger Indians; however, it is still necessary that the older members be taken into consideration and assisted in a manner by which they can maintain their self-respect in a type of livelihood with which they are acquainted.
Since the hon. minister assumed office she has caused action to be taken for the construction of a new school at Old Crow. This is extremely commendable. The school is being constructed not only with native materials but with native labour. This will put substantial numbers of breadwinners into this area to work; work which is vitally required at this particular time of the year in view of the fact that in the last year and a half the fur industry has dropped to a new low, thereby severely restricting the range of income which these people have at their disposal. This type of program is recommended for other such projects which are required in other like areas, but in the meantime it is necessary to consider the remoter areas, such as Ross river, and consider the feasibility of following the advice of the legislative council of the Yukon, as well as the commissioner-I may add my own opinion to that-regarding the implementation of these welfare payments in the form of wolf bounties in the remoter areas. This is a new approach to the matter of a wolf bounty. It is not a question of a handout but of a monetary payment in the form of a welfare grant which, at the same time, assists in the control of predatory animals.
I pass on quickly to the matter of children's aid. I believe the hon. minister was presented with a brief by the Southern Yukon
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Children's Aid Society. This is an organization which was formed recently. When I say recently, I should say in the last three or four years. This organization has done more to alleviate suffering and hardship among the infant population in the Yukon than any other organization of which I am aware. This is an organization which until now has been entirely supported by private subscription; that is to say, it has had no connection with the government. A surprising fact is that 74.6 per cent of the cases that were handled by this society during the period January, 1958 to October, 1958 were cases involving Indian children, Indians of white status or halfbreeds. At the moment this organization is gaining support only by private subscription. The brief which was presented by the children's aid society asked for government financial help. I think, Mr. Chairman, this is a matter which deserves the very special consideration of the minister. I simply quote the last paragraph of the brief which was presented in order to show the need for the immediate consideration of the request made by this organization. It reads:
Though we have never previously requested financial aid from the department, the society now has to request an annual grant, despite generous contributions from the public. Our work has increased four-fold, necessitating additional paid help, rental of an office, and many other expenses. Our whole program is expanding and we will need more financial support from the departments of the government we are serving. The amount we are asking is $3,000 annually. A brief has been submitted to the territorial government requesting an increase in our annual grant, and if we fail in our efforts to obtain these, our treasurer reports that we shall be forced to cease to function after May 1959.
I commend this request to the minister's special consideration, because without such aid the society, as it has said, will be forced to discontinue this work. I know that the minister and all hon. members will agree that this is an effort that is deserving of every possible support.
I should like to conclude my remarks by referring to the minutes of a conference of Indian delegates which was held at Whitehorse on June 10, 1958. I believe the director of the branch, who has done such wonderful work in the Yukon in the last two years, was in attendance at that meeting. The Indian delegates who represented their various bands at this meeting brought up matters ranging from housing, education and aid to trappers, to bounties and refrigeration. In fact, the whole field of Indian affairs was covered. Two or three of the outstanding features of the ensuing brief deserve particular consideration.
One refers to the fact that unemployment insurance is not now available to two classes

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of Indian people in the Yukon, and I assume this also applies elsewhere. The first class of people affected are Indian trappers, and the second are those engaged in forest firefighting duties. The Indian people feel that unemployment insurance should be paid to Indian people who are engaged in trapping and firefighting on the same basis as it is paid to those engaged in fishing. They believe that when trappers or firefighters are out of work they are entitled to receive unemployment insurance.
There is one further matter which is of some importance and which I should like to include as having been among the subjects dealt with, at the meeting on December 29, by the legislators of the territorial council. This concerns the need for an Indian placement officer, and a recommendation to this effect was unanimously supported at that meeting. Again I say that this represents the view of the Commissioner of the territory and of the five members of the Legislative Council of the Yukon, in addition to the heads of the two main branches of the church up there, and many other people. Bishop Coudert who is the bishop of the Roman Catholic church in the Yukon, said specifically that there is a need for a placement officer in the Yukon agency. This particular request was also made by the various Indian people who made up the delegation which attended the meeting last July. Bishop Coudert also stated that there is a need for the Indians and halfbreeds in the Whitehorse area to be provided with additional houses. I know that the minister is making progress in this regard, and I should like to commend her on this work.
Bishop Greenwood of the Anglican church reiterated the need for an Indian placement officer. He said, further, that the care of old and disabled Indian people presented a problem. He also expressed the feeling that steps should be taken in order to permit the inclusion in the bands of some illegitimate children of Indian women born between September 1951 and August 1956 in addition to legally adopted children. This is very important because unless these people are classified as Indians they cannot attend the schools set up specifically for Indian children; they are neither white nor Indian as far as the definition given in the Indian Act is concerned. Unless they fall within the definition given in the act they are denied the right of access to the Indian schools. They are also being denied the right of access to the hostels which are being constructed at the moment in Whitehorse, so

they cannot come into Whitehorse from outlying points and attend the new schools, because they have no place in which to live.
There is a very pressing need for something to be done about this situation. It is something which requires immediate attention. I think this view has been expressed by Commissioner Collins and by others in the Yukon and I would suggest that the minister give this matter every consideration prior to the opening of these new hostels and the school in Whitehorse, because otherwise these children would be denied the educational facilities which are being provided.
One further thing which came out of this meeting last June at which the director was in attendance was a statement by an Indian delegate that more liaison work could be done with regard to the integration of the Indian people into jobs in industry. This, once again, emphasizes the need for the establishment of an Indian placement officer in the Yukon. It seems odd that there should be more government employees concerned with the administration of forests and wild life in the Yukon than are concerned with the welfare of the Indian people. I trust the situation will not continue to be as it has been over the past 30 years.
With regard to the question of freezers there are, I believe, two freezers being built in the Yukon in different locations, but there is need for one in Dawson. Perhaps I could do no better here than quote from the remarks which were made last June at the conference which was held with the chief of the Dawson band. The latter said this absence of freezer facilities was a matter for regret. Apropos of this, an amusing story was told by Chief Charlie Mason. An Indian agent once had locker-freezers built in two places. One was not a place where a freezer was needed. An Indian from a place that needed a freezer locker said, "Why did you build one in that town?" The agent said, "I made a mistake". The Indian said, "I wish you would make a mistake and build one in our place." Dawson natives hope that soon a mistake will be made and a freezer put in Dawson for the native people commented Chief Mason.
I could do no better than conclude with the words of that chief as set out in these minutes:
It would seem that the native wants many things. It is true. He feels he has been robbed of his land and his livelihood and not much has been given in return. He feels that nobody cares much for his adjustment to the new way of life. Some people work and help but they have not the money or the time or the authority to do much. The native needs more understanding. We feel we should have an assistant agent living in Dawson who will be with us from day to day. The agent

could help us and teach us better and make us happier. Our people are getting more and more in number every year. The agent should be able to give us help now before the problems get too big.
Chief Mason continues:
Sometimes the agent says he is too busy in Whitehorse to come to Dawson. The department is like the candidate for parliament who visited Old Crow.
I may say that the chief is not speaking about me here, he is speaking about my then opponent.
He got off the plane. He said to the people "I am sorry I am late. For five days there was bad weather." One of the men said, "That is too bad. Did you have bad weather for the nine years before that?"
Mr. Jutras helps us out a lot and is thinking a great deal about us, but the head of his department should give him authority to put a man in Dawson. For too long the government has been away from us and has not come to help us. Mr. Meek was a good agent too, but he needed more help. So we think it is important to have an agent or representative for the agent in Dawson.
I thank you for listening to this our letter from Dawson natives. We hope that you will consider it with sympathy.
These are not isolated ideas, but are common and shared by all the Indian people of the Yukon. The problems have been stated before and I commend them to the minister for her sympathetic attention.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to what was said concerning the people at Old Crow by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat may I say that I am sure he knows these people come under the Indian agency which is in part of my riding and I am sure from now on they will looked after properly and very well.
Before the evening recess the minister replied to some of the suggestions I proposed early in the afternoon. I noted that she said there was some merit in the hiring of works foremen in the various settlements in the north. I wonder if the minister would give an opinion as to some of the other suggestions I made. In particular I should like to have her comments on my suggestion concerning the payment of salaries to Indian chiefs who would work in co-operation with the works foremen in selling government policy to the native Indians. I am sure the minister and the officials of the department realize how valuable it would be to have the co-operation of the chiefs in these settlements when projects are undertaken which are aimed at bringing the Indians out of their present condition into a better world.

Mr. Chairman, may I interrupt the hon. member. He raised the subject on the first item of this department, No. 56, and I did answer him at that time. True enough, I did not deal with every suggestion
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration he made but I suggest to him that he is now re-hashing an item which has been passed. All of the suggestions he made will be considered by the department.
At this moment, Mr. Chairman, I am uncertain whether we are considering item No. 59 or 60. I thought No. 59 was passed but it appeared to me that the hon. member for the Yukon was directing his remarks entirely to No. 60. Possibly we could straighten that out now.
I do not wish to disagree with the minister or with the Chair but I believe we are considering item No. 59 at the present time.

If we are on No. 59, Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I thought we had passed that item but since we are still on it perhaps I could tell the hon. gentleman that we can only estimate the backlog of estates. About three years ago there were approximately 9,000 and it has now been reduced to approximately 5,000. I am expressing this in round figures, of course. The hon. gentleman will understand that it is a little difficult for us to arrive at an exact figure. To do so would require careful review of a large number of old estates. Sometimes when a new estate is opened it in turn reflects upon or has some bearing upon an old estate until a few matters are cleared up concerning the old estate, and so on. While not entirely satisfactory the figures show a rather remarkable improvement over the last three years, let us say.

The minister is quite
satisfied now that she has a good organization for dealing with this?
Yes.
When I was minister I often said I was thoroughly dissatisfied with the situation and I attempted to do a great deal to improve it. I am glad to hear it is working itself out.
I am sure the hon. member will understand that once you start to improve a thing it snowballs-
I am only too happy to take the credit, Mr. Chairman.
I might say it looks very encouraging now. We are on our way to cutting a large slice out of this backlog and I believe over a period of time it will eventually come down to a much smaller figure.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that some of the questions I asked this afternoon relating to the welfare of Indians have not been answered and I wonder if the minister will consider this an appropriate item under which to comment on those matters?

Mr. Chairman, at six
o'clock I checked all my notes and I thought I had answered the hon. member in every respect except in a couple of instances where the hon. gentleman raised questions that obviously I could not answer off the cuff. It is necessary to have consultation with the department on some of these matters. I cannot give him an offhand answer on some of these issues. As far as I am aware I have answered every question he posed that could possibly be answered orally.
I wish now to say a few words with respect to the questions raised by the hon. member for the Yukon who made some serious suggestions. I might tell him the matter of unemployment insurance does not come under the jurisdiction of this department and he will have to raise his questions when the estimates of the Department of Labour are called. We are attempting to have placement officers stationed at all places where they may be usefully employed. We are gradually placing them in areas where they have not been placed heretofore and I hope we will get around to the Yukon shortly.
The matter of co-operation with the children's aid society is under active consideration and I think will come to a successful conclusion very shortly.
Is the hon. lady going to tell me about my cash relief, Mr. Chairman?
Mr. Chairman, I thought I had dealt with that question early in the afternoon. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would care to repeat his question.
If the hon. lady has dealt with it, I apologize. I was out of the chamber for a little while and she may have answered it during my absence.

Mr. Chairman, with all due deference may I say that I was present this afternoon and I cannot recall that the hon. lady commented on several of the suggestions I offered. I should like to have her comments on my proposal with regard to her department supplying to the Department of Transport a list of graduates from vocational training schools who could operate equipment for that and other departments on contract work. I should like to have her speak about my suggestion concerning the payment of a salary to Indian chiefs who 

would work as, shall I say, straw bosses or assistants to the works foremen. I do not recall that she gave an opinion with respect to my proposal about having the Department of Fisheries conduct surveys on inland lakes to see if they are suitable for commercial fishing by Indians. There was also the suggestion about providing equipment to assist Indians wishing to engage in commercial fishing on Great Slave lake and other related questions.

Mr. Chairman, with respect I submit that I did answer those questions in a general way. The hon. member knows that I cannot answer for other departments of government. I did tell him that every suggestion he made would be very carefully considered. Some of the suggestions he made I am sure he himself in all fairness would not expect me to answer immediately without consultation with my department and without full consideration of the implications of some of the rather drastic ones that he did make. As to some of the suggestions he made, I would ask him to give the department a chance to digest what he has asked and not press for an answer now because, in any event, I cannot give an answer particularly to problems which have interdepartmental implications.

Mr. Chairman, I will take for granted that the minister agreed with what I said. I personally did not think that some of the questions, particularly those in regard to employment by the Department of Transport in the filling of vacancies and so on, were answered but I will look forward to reading Hansard tomorrow to see what the minister did say in this respect.

Possibly I did not answer that particular one, but I can tell the hon. member that this department has circularized to all departments of government a plea to employ Indians wherever possible. We have met with considerable success in a great many parts of the country. I do not think any steps have yet been taken with regard to circularizing subcontractors but we are taking that into consideration. I can assure him that this department is pressing as hard as it can to employ Indians wherever possible in the areas in which they are resident.
I asked this afternoon whether a placement officer would be located in the Northwest Territories.
I answered that really when I was answering the hon. member for the Yukon. We are hopeful of placing officers in those various sections of the country as quickly as possible.

62. Operation and maintenance including an amount of $5,700 for grants to promote Indian agriculture, handicrafts and economic enterprises generally, $867,272.

The hon. lady knows exactly what I am going to ask her on this item. I want to know whether a successor has yet been appointed to Mr. Mel Jack, and whether she is satisfied with him and what is he doing?

Mr. Chairman, I am very sorry to say that there has been no successor appointed as yet. I am most regretful about that. We have held two competitions but, as the hon. member very well knows, this is a position which requires a peculiar kind of specialized background. He was fortunate enough to secure a man who had that kind of background. If he can suggest to me one who can take his place I can assure him that I will treat his suggestion with the greatest consideration because I would like to find someone right at the moment who could really do the job.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Resources to take over this responsibility of economic development of Indians in the Northwest Territories I would hope that she would make it very plain to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that we do not want any long-haired Ph.D.'s. You are hired.

I still hope the minister will say a little about it. Has it been a success?

We think it has been a success. The only thing that bothers me about these scholarships is that there are not enough of them. I feel very strongly on this and I have said to many people in important places that there is a great deal of latent talent among the Indians. If the Leader of the Opposition will permit me, I have a short statement I would like to make with reference to the national gallery.
It has been known since the spring of 1955 that the national gallery would move to the Lome building some time during 1959. It is now confirmed that the move will take place on or about September 30.
The move to the new building will have a number of important results in terms of services to the public, both Canadian and tourist. All of the important works in the collection will be on public view; there will be space, at last, to show and properly to house the print and drawing collection, which is one of the finest in terms of quality in North America; there will be sufficient room to show a reasonable proportion of the war collections; all the important works in the sculpture collection, which is a small one, will be on view. We will have our own auditorium and we will be able to present a greatly increased and far more systematic program of public lectures, film programs, and so forth. There will be sufficient space for the scientific and conservation laboratory to develop and expand into a truly national service; the design centre will return to its old site at the corner of Albert and Slater; the library and photographic library service will have sufficient space for these services to operate at a level worthy of a national gallery; the workshop area in the double basement will allow the extension and travelling exhibition services to operate with proper efficiency. Perhaps the greatest gain of all is that special exhibitions can be mounted without displacing the permanent collection.
The prospect of the move to a new building has affected the work and program of the gallery profoundly over the past four years. The staff has been slowly increased- it is now almost double what it was in 1955- as people could be found and trained for both the increased curatorial work which will result from a much greater proportion of the national collection being on public view and also to deal with a greatly expanded extension program serving some 120 centres across the country.

Mr. Chairman, the committee, I think, will have learned with satisfaction of the progress made in the transfer of the gallery to its new building, a project which was initiated, as the minister knows, some few years ago before she was so happily in charge of the department.
While I congratulate the minister on that progress report, I am afraid I cannot congratulate her in regard to a matter which I wish to bring up at this time, undoubtedly not to her surprise, and which is concerned with the possible purchase or negotiations for the purchase of a picture for the gallery, a Breughel.
I think I should begin by pointing out to the committee that I believe the minister was not in charge of the department after the change of government when negotiations for the purchase of this picture began, and therefore she does not have any direct responsibility perhaps for the sorry, unhappy ending of these negotiations. I have had the opportunity of making some investigation into this matter and, as I have just said, it is a confused, unhappy situation which brings no credit to the government and which, on the contrary, has resulted in a good deal of discredit to the government and to the name of Canada in those circles which are concerned with art matters.
What I am dealing with is not the desirability or otherwise of spending a large sum of money at this time for the purchase of a picture, however rare and beautiful that picture may be. The question at issue is the way in which this matter was handled or rather mishandled, as I see it, by the government. The reply by the minister, to be found on page 1364 of Hansard for February 25, to a question put on the order paper by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate concerning this matter certainly does not mitigate the complaint that we have to make with regard to the way the matter was dealt with.
If I am inaccurate in giving my account of these negotiations no doubt the minister, who has the records at her disposal, will correct me. As I understand the situation, the first contact between a representative of the gallery and the agent for the owner of the picture, a landscape by Breughel, was made on January 4, 1957, when the gallery became interested in what perhaps is one of the finest pictures of its kind in the world and one of the very few pictures of this artistic value which was open for purchase. I believe that in January of 1957 a value of approximately $500,000 was placed on the picture by the European owner.
A good many months later, on October 22, 1957, after the election of that year, I believe
1904	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the owner of the picture or the agent of the owner was informed that the trustees of the national gallery, who would naturally have to pass on any purchase of a picture of this kind or any other kind, were interested and I believe the director was authorized at that time to pursue the matter further and no doubt report back. I am informed that in October of 1957 the amount involved was far beyond the appropriation of the national gallery.
However, in December, 1957, the officers of the gallery, no doubt with authority, pursued the question of price with the owner or the agent of the owner of the picture. I am informed that in January, 1958 the agent for the owner of the picture was told that the trustees of the national gallery of Canada had unanimously expressed the intention to acquire this painting if negotiations could be satisfactorily concluded, that negotiations then began with the owner or agent on the question of price and that late in January, 1958 the owner was then informed that there would be a delay because of the political situation in Canada and the approach of an election and nothing could be worked out very quickly on that account.
But in February the agent did learn that the trustees were pursuing the matter of the purchase and that question was before the government at that time for a definite opinion on whether or not the picture should be bought. Then, toward the end of April the owner or agent was informed that the trustees of the national gallery had agreed on a figure which, if other aspects of the matter could be cleared up, might be offered to the owner, that figure being $350,000, well below the amount I have quoted as being the value placed on the picture some time earlier by the owner. It was considerably less than that earlier value.
I have already referred to the answer given by the minister to the question asked in the house. As found on page 1364 of Hansard the minister made this reply:
-the board of trustees of the national gallery had asked-
Presumably had asked the government.
-for "authorization to negotiate for the purchase of the Breughel owned by Baron von Polnitz". At the same time the trustees asserted that the necessary funds had been appropriated and were available for the purchase. This statement was confirmed by the director of the gallery.
I gather from that that the government got their information as to the availability of funds for this picture not from any treasury board authority, not from the Department of Finance but from the officers of the national gallery, from the director and trustees of the national gallery. Having received their


information not from treasury board but from the trustees and the director of the national gallery, according to the answer to this question, that money was available, on the basis of that information the cabinet on May 2 authorized the Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to give permission to the director to proceed accordingly. Apparently, by that it meant to proceed with the negotiations for the purchase of the picture.
I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that on the other end of the deal a very different understanding prevailed. I am informed that the agent for the owner was told by the director of the gallery that he was authorized, not merely to negotiate as stated in the answer to this question but to make an offer of $350,000 for this picture, presumably on the understanding that this money was available, on the basis of information secured from the gallery itself and not from the treasury board or the Department of Finance or the other authorities of government which might be expected to know.
He was authorized to make an offer, authorized by the government to make an offer of this amount without any strings attached, with payment to be made on delivery of the picture sometime after May 12. The agent was asked, as a matter of urgency, to get a reply from the owner. He got in touch with the owner on May 3 and the owner assumed that this was an offer made in good faith, a valid offer, without any strings attached. The owner accepted the offer and the agent wired the director of the gallery accordingly and requested, I am informed, written confirmation.
Then on May 5 the director of the gallery told the agent that he would send a purchase contract in a few days and payment would be made. There would be a little delay in making payment because it would have to wait until after parliament convened, but that would be a mere formality. Then three days later the director, after all these negotiations had been completed, informed the agent that there would be difficulty in regard to the financing of this picture because the cabinet had authorized this firm offer on the understanding that the money was readily available from some fund which was in existence for the purchase of pictures from the Liechtenstein collection. Now they discovered, after this firm offer had been made, that there was no such money readily available from that fund. The agent was informed that it was hoped this difficulty would soon be cleared up and the contract could be signed.

It was not until four or five days after that, on May 12 or May 13, that finally the agent for the owner of this picture was able to see the minister concerned, and the minister then explained that this was all very unfortunate; that there had been a misunderstanding; that the money which was thought to be available was not available and therefore the deal, if I may put it this way, was off and no purchase would be made.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that, according to my information, is an account of the events leading up to the decision of the government, first to authorize the firm offer and eventually to withdraw that firm offer and tell the owner of the picture that the deal was off. Perhaps in the present circumstances it was a very wise decision not to spend the money for the picture at this time-I am not qualified to judge-but surely, the way this was done reflects no credit on anybody concerned with it. I am sure it has given Canada a very bad name in circles which deal in art matters. Perhaps this may not be of any immediate importance to Canadians but it will do Canada no good in future when we wish to add valuable pictures to our national gallery.
Perhaps I could complete this sorry record of mishandling by asking the minister, who would no doubt wish to reply to what I have said, whether at any time the owner has, since this date I have mentioned of May 13, asked for an interview with the Prime Minister or any minister to get an explanation why this matter was handled in this way? Has the minister any other information she could give to us about this matter which, as I have already said and I repeat, was an unfortunate example of confusion, fumbling, bumbling and mishandling.

May I preface my remarks by saying I have no apology to make for the action of the government with regard to this particular matter. The Leader of the Opposition has seen fit to read into the record his own assumptions with respect to what might have taken place in the negotiations for the purchase of the Breughel. I made my statement in the house, as he has said, on February 25, after due consideration. I should like to quote the last two paragraphs of that statement in which I said:
It is clear that no authority existed to make a firm offer or enter into a contract for this purchase by the national gallery or the government of Canada or anyone on its or their behalf. The Financial Administration Act specifically requires that there be an appropriation provided by parliament for the purpose before a contract can be made.
It is reiterated that the authority asked for was to negotiate. Although granted in the first instance this was immediately revoked as soon as the lack of appropriation was revealed.
Business of the House
The Leader of the Opposition has been at some pains to castigate the government for its lack of knowledge of what funds had been appropriated. But the Leader of the Opposition has been a minister of the crown as well as a deputy minister, and I think he knows that the minister relies upon information which is given to him by his officials.
I also know that the minister takes responsibility for all acts of his officials.

That is all well and good; then, is the Leader of the Opposition suggesting to me now that he is castigating the government or is he casting reflections upon the director of the national gallery or upon the board of trustees?

I will answer that question. I am casting reflections upon the government which must take the responsibility for the way these negotiations were conducted. Perhaps the minister, if she thinks my information is wrong, will table all the correspondence in connection with this matter, all the letters, telegrams, records of telephone calls and any material which will throw any light on this situation?

If the Leader of the Opposition wishes to request in specific terms what he requires to be tabled we will be glad to look into it. I would say to him that because of his long experience in government, both as a civil servant and as a minister of the crown, he knows very well that the government has no power to spend funds which have not been appropriated.
They should find that out.
The minister should know that before making any commitments.

There was no appropriation and, as the Leader of the Opposition stated, this did not happen during my term of office. I will say that I would not condone the expenditure of funds and I would not ask parliament to provide funds to cover up a fiasco like this.

subsubtopic: QUALIFICATIONS OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
What qualities and qualifications are desirable in a director of: (a) the human history branch of the national museum of Canada; (b) the natural history branch of the national museum of Canada?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilion (Minister of
Northern Affairs and National Resources):
(a) and (b). In addition to good health and personal suitability, the desirable qualities in a director of either branch of the national museum of Canada comprise a sound knowledge of and capacity for management and administration, organizational ability, and capacity to co-ordinate research. Specific qualifications include:	graduation with a
doctor's degree from a university of recognized standing with specialization in one or more of the related fields; extensive experience in one or more of the disciplines involved and an international standing as shown by published results; experience in planning, exhibits and a knowledge of modern museum and public information methods. In the case of a director of the human history branch, it might be expected to find a candidate with specialization and experience in fields or disciplines such as anthropology, ethnology or archaeology. In the case of a director of the natural history branch it might be expected to find a candidate with specialization and experience in fields or disciplines such as geology, minerology, palaeontology, zoology or botany.

4.	If so, for what reason or reasons have they been disregarded?
5.	Have steps been taken to implement any of these recommendations in the near future?
6.	If so, which ones?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister
of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	Yes.
2.	The text may be found on pages 323 and 324 of the royal commission's report.
3.	Yes.

1.	The best evidence available shows that the existing Canadian radioactivity testing program compares most favourably with those of other leading countries in the nuclear field. A study of the report of the United Nations scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation of August, 1958, confirms this view. Since the beginning of this program in 1955, the Department of National Health and Welfare has built a new radiochemical building in Ottawa, the number of scientific and technical positions has been substantially increased and at this very moment the department is broadening the scope of its investigations to include measurements of radioactivity in rainfall, air and soil. The program is further supported by the recent construction of two whole-body measuring units for the determination of radioactivity in humans. The department has planned to build a third Canadian unit of this type which it considers an essential part of the studies.
The department is keeping abreast of all new scientific developments in this field and to this end the program is kept under constant review.
2.	Excessive levels of strontium 90 have occurred only on nuclear weapon testing sites, of which there is none in Canada. On the basis of findings of the Department of National Health and Welfare there is at present no discernible hazard by strontium 90 contamination of milk.

speechtext:
May I, in the absence through illness of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, make on his behalf an announcement concerning a Canadian aid program in southeast Asia. The announcement is being made simultaneously elsewhere.
For a number of years the United Nations commission for Asia and the Far East has been conducting a series of investigations and studies of the development possibilities of the lower Mekong river basin. The Mekong is one of the great rivers of the world. Its total length is about 2,600 miles, and its length in the lower basin is 1,600 miles. It actually rises in southern China but for most of its course it flows through or between
Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and South Viet Nam. The economic health and the political stability and independence of these countries are in large measure related to this great river.
The development of the lower Mekong offers great economic benefits to the four riparian states and, indeed, to the region as a whole, in terms of flood control, irrigation, hydroelectric power and improved navigation. The realization of these benefits, however, is still many years away. Some preliminary planning and survey work has been done but further progress cannot be made without first obtaining more reliable and detailed data on the basin. The development possibilities are so encouraging that the United States, New Zealand, France, Japan and several agencies of the United Nations have already contributed men and resources to carry out these further investigations.
For our own part, while the bulk of Canada's aid under the Colombo plan has been and should be concentrated in commonwealth countries, the government considered that this project was sufficiently challenging and promised such great benefits as to warrant some Canadian participation in it. Moreover, the government was influenced by the fact that these benefits would go in substantial degree to countries with which Canada has been closely associated in recent years through our membership in the international supervisory commissions in Indochina.
We therefore made available the services of Lieutenant Colonel G. S. Andrews, surveyor general of the department of lands and forests of the province of British Columbia, to make a detailed study of the problems and estimated costs involved in the aerial surveying and mapping of the Mekong river which, as hon. members will appreciate, is an essential first step toward the eventual realization of the potential benefits of this project.
On the basis of Colonel Andrews' report the Canadian government has now decided to participate in the first priority phase of the survey and mapping of the main stem of the Mekong river. This work, which Canadian companies are particularly well qualified to undertake, is expected to extend over two years and will involve an aggregate Canadian contribution of up to $1.3 million. It is the intention of the government to finance

Announced Canadian Aid to Southeast Asia this contribution from Colombo plan funds which parliament will be asked to appropriate in 1959-60 and 1960-61.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT CONCERNING IMPOSITION OF TOLLS  TABLING OF NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
make a statement regarding the agreement reached between Canada and the United States on the tolls to be charged on the St. Lawrence seaway. With the concurrence of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I now table copies in English and in French of the exchange of notes dated March 9, 1959, constituting an agreement between the Canadian and United States governments. The agreement makes provision for the division of the toll revenue, for the method of collection, for future minor amendments of the tariff and for the constitution of a joint tolls advisory board to hear complaints with respect to interpretation of the tariff or alleged unjust discrimination.
The tariff becomes effective from April 1, 1959. The whole concept of defraying the cost of construction and maintenance of the seaway, including the cost of deepening and maintaining the Welland canal as an integral part of the seaway by charging tolls, was provided for in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act of 1951. This principle was fully debated at that time and passed without dissent by parliament.
The tariff of tolls agreed to has the same rates recommended by the tolls committees of the seaway entities on June 12, 1958. Some changes and clarifications have been made in the definitions of bulk and general cargoes.

Statement on St. Lawrence Seaway Tolls
The tariff of tolls is based on a composite assessment which encompasses a charge per ton of cargo actually carried together with a charge per gross registered ton of the vessel, and will be applicable to all vessels whether laden, partially laden or in ballast.
The method of assessing and collecting the tolls and rates was adopted with the following objectives: one, procedural simplicity which will minimize the cost of collection and expedite the dispatching of vessels; two, recovery of the cost of the seaway and its operation on a basis which will provide economic rates to users and encourage traffic.
The rates will be as follows: 1. A vessel will be assessed 6 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 42 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 95 cents per ton of general cargo carried. 2. A vessel will be assessed 4 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 40 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 90 cents per ton of general cargo carried. For partial transit of the new seaway facilities between Montreal and lake Ontario, where there are seven locks, the user will be charged for each lock transited 15 per cent of the toll for complete passage.
3.	For each passage through the Welland canal only a vessel will be assessed 2 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel and, in addition, 2 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 5 cents per ton of general cargo carried. In the Welland canal a partial transit will be assessed 50 per cent of the toll for complete passage irrespective of the number of locks used.
Other main features of the agreement and tariff of tolls are: First of all, commercial vessels carrying passengers will be charged 50 cents per passenger for each lock transited between Montreal and lake Erie, in addition to the vessel and cargo charge. The charge for a complete transit of the seaway will be $7.50 per passenger. The tariff will apply to all types of craft using the seaway, including government owned or government operated vessels except vessels of or employed by the seaway entities. Pleasure craft will be subject to the same rates as other vessels except that there is a minimum charge for pleasure craft of $2 per lock transited. The minimum charge for all other vessels will be $4 per lock transited.
The unit of weight for the collection of tolls will be a ton of 2,000 pounds. Provision is made for prior registration of vessels and satisfactory security to be given for the payment of charges subsequent to which passage will be permitted. Toll collection and invoicing of accounts, as well as the preparation of statistical data, are assigned to the St. Lawrence seaway authority at Cornwall. The
66968-9-118
St. Lawrence seaway development corporation will participate in the billing and collecting operation and will share in the annual cost of these services. Charges will be billed to the ship owner or representative promptly and will be payable within 14 days of the date of billing. An additional charge for non-payment within this period may be levied in an amount not to exceed 5 per cent of the amount due.
For through passages to or from Montreal and lake Ontario the invoice will show two amounts to be paid; 1, Canadian funds to cover the portion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway authority of Canada, which has been intially set at 71 per cent of the total charges, and 2, the balance of the account, or 29 per cent, in United States funds representing the portion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation. Tolls for passage on the Welland canal will be paid in Canadian funds only.
Bulk cargo as defined in the tariff of tolls includes such goods as are loose or in mass and generally must be shovelled, pumped, blown, scooped or forked in the handling and, without limiting the generality of the term or otherwise affecting its meaning, it is deemed to include barley, buckwheat, corn, dried beans, dried peas, flaxseed, rapeseed and other seeds, flour, grain screenings, mill feed containing not more than 35 per cent of ingredients other than grain or grain products, oats, rye and wheat, loose or in sacks; cement, loose or in sacks; coke and petroleum coke, loose or in sacks; domestic package freight; liquids carried in ships' tanks; ores and minerals, loose or in sacks, including alumina, bauxite, coke, gravel, phosphate rock, sand, stone and sulphur; pig iron, scrap iron and scrap steel; pulpwood, poles and logs, loose or bundled; raw sugar, loose or in sacks; and wood pulp, loose or in bales. All commodities not included in the definition of "bulk" are classified as general cargo.
The agreement provides that the toll revenue for that portion of the seaway between Montreal and lake Ontario be shared proportionately to the annual charges of the two seaway entities. The agreement also permits, under appropriate procedure, changes in the list of goods defined as bulk cargo.
The joint tolls advisory board to be constituted will consist of four persons, two of whom shall be appointed by the St. Lawrence seaway authority and two by the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation. The board will hear complaints relating to the interpretation of the tariff by the authority or the corporation, or with respect to alleged unjust discrimination arising out of the
1862	HOUSE OF
Statement on St. Lawrence Seaway Tolls operation of the tariff, and report its findings and recommendations to the authority and the corporation.
The two seaway entities are charged with the duty of reporting to their respective governments not later than July 1, 1964 as to the sufficiency of the authorized tolls to meet the statutory requirements and to cause the tariff to be reviewed accordingly. Reviews of the tariff at other times may, of course, take place by decision of the two governments.
As hon. members know, this great inland waterway will become operative with the opening of the navigation season this year, and we have every reason to look forward to a material increase in the volume of shipping using these facilities. This should be of great assistance to the development of the commerce of this country as a whole, and should enable goods produced in Canada to become more competitive in world markets. We look forward to the whole economy of Canada benefiting with the opening of this great seaway project.

[Mr. Hees.l

We are unable to assess fully, from the information received, the impact of this agreement on the various sections of Canada or on certain industries, agricultural producers and so on. We will therefore have to reserve our objective and informed comments until a later date.

We realize that in those circumstances we cannot have all we want if we are to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement. We do hope the government has done its very best in securing this agreement to protect the interests of all sections of Canada. We all know, I think, that the government has received representations from certain provincial governments in Canada, and possibly from some sections of industry, urging a toll free St. Lawrence seaway. I was pleased to note, while listening to the minister's statement, that there is provision in the agreement for consideration of complaints by persons concerned to the board authority. I do hope they take every advantage of that provision in the agreement to bring to the attention of the government the views of various industries, producers and users of the canal across Canada with the idea that as time proceeds the arrangements under this agreement will be satisfactory to all sections of the Canadian people.
In conclusion I want to mention that these requests which have come from various provinces and certain industries and producers in Canada for free tolls spring from the increasing costs of transportation in Canada at this time; that is their basis. I think the protests and the whole argument in support of free tolls are convincing evidence of the necessity of the establishment of a national transportation policy in Canada at the earliest possible date.

I would rather see a larger maximum allowable, to take into account particular circumstances.
I should like to raise one other matter. It has to do with our general attitude toward Indians, which I hope will change as we progress. Generally we in Canada look with abhorrence upon racial discrimination which exists in other parts of the world. We decry the attitude that exists in certain sections of the United States toward its negro population. We view with distaste the approach of apartheid in certain parts of the world such as Africa. Generally we pride ourselves on being free from discrimination in Canadaj and we say that other countries certainly are not as far advanced in racial equality as we are.
I do not think we should pride ourselves too much on that, because there still exists in a number of places in Canada, consciously or otherwise, an attitude of discrimination against native Canadian peoples in terms of providing them with employment and accommodation in hotels and things of that nature. I know we cannot legislate, though we have tried it in some provinces in Canada, to make that type of discrimination illegal, because it is an attitude of mind on the part of one group as against another. I only express the hope that in the future we shall think more in terms of an attitude of equality toward our native Indian people, far more so than we have done in the past.
I should like to deal with one other specific item. Inasmuch as we shall be establishing a joint committee of this house and the other place shortly-at least I hope it will be shortly-there will be ample opportunity to go in the fullest possible detail into the problems of our native Indian peoples, and I hope we shall find some solutions to them. Therefore my remarks will be rather general and brief on this occasion.
There is a question affecting our native Indian peoples, namely the question of liquor as it relates to the native Indian, that I should like to deal with. On March 4 there was a news item in the Vancouver Province which apparently arose out of a letter that a Mr. Andy Pauli from Vancouver had sent to the minister, asking that native Indians there be given the right to buy liquor in liquor stores and also packaged goods-they are called that-in liquor stores and take them home. The announcement of the attorney general of British Columbia was to the effect that the first move, in so far as liquor rights for Indians were concerned, was entirely up to the Indians themselves.
I suppose in the strict and narrow sense, without taking into account the full provisions of the Indian Act in so far as liquor

is concerned, the attorney general was correct. But I think someone should either bring him up to date on what the law of this country is, or he should go back to law school for a little while to find out what is in the Indian Act; because the attitude of the attorney general in that province is not conducive to providing equality of opportunity for our native Indian peoples.
He says that in the first instance it is up to the Indians themselves. I would point out the ridiculous situation which would exist if Indian band councils were to take advantage of a section of the Indian Act having to do with the right to have liquor on the Indian reserves without having the right to be in possession of liquor in other parts of the province. An Indian band council could do this under a section of the Indian Act. If they took that action and the attorney general of British Columbia, or the attorney general of any other province, did not object within 60 days; if they had a referendum and the reserve decided that they wanted the right to consume liquor on the reserve, we would find that they would be in the ridiculous position of having the right to consume liquor on the reserve but no right to buy it or to keep it there. They would have the right to drink in a beer parlour, as they have in British Columbia, but they could not buy a case of beer in a beer parlour and take it home on the reserve, where they could have the right to have it if they were to follow the suggestion of the attorney general.
So far as British Columbia and the other provinces are concerned, the matter rests squarely on the shoulders of the provincial governments from the point of view of taking the initiative. Certainly Indian band councils could take the initiative but, as I am sure the minister realizes, that would merely promote a chaotic situation.
Our liquor laws as they relate to Indians are a bit foolish. We hear the comment that Indian people cannot handle their liquor, that they do all sorts of wild things when they have access to liquor, and therefore we should not allow them to have it or, if we do, only under strict conditions. It is quite true that when a native Indian gets a little too much of the corn under his belt he becomes drunk, obnoxious, loud-mouthed, sloppy, argumentative and wants to fight. It is quite true that is what happens to the native Indian; in fact he is almost as bad as the white man who does the same thing. There is no difference.
I should like to point out the ridiculousness of our liquor laws as they apply to native Indians. Depending on who and 66968-9-119

In the past Frank Calder, by reason of the position he then held as a member of the legislature, was invited to a number of receptions. He was an Indian, a member of a band and prohibited from drinking liquor, but he was invited to a number of receptions and he went. The R.C.M.P. were there and they did not interfere in any way. Yet Frank Calder broke the law respecting liquor rights as much as it was possible to break the law. I do not blame him one bit; I would do the same thing myself if I were in his position. Again, not only at the reception I have mentioned but at every session of the provincial legislature Frank Calder was invited to a reception by the lieutenant governor of the province.
There is another awkward relationship involving a native Indian and the liquor laws. It has to do with a gentleman who is a member of the other place. Because of his background, because of his race, because of the position he holds, no doubt he has been invited to many receptions in the past at which liquor was served and undoubtedly he will be invited to similar receptions in the future. As the situation stands now, having regard to the province of Ontario only, if that hon. gentleman as a member of the other house accepts an invitation to such a reception he is in order. He is not contravening the law.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member cannot refer to the actions of a member of the other place in the present fashion. Furthermore, all references concerning various guests whom the lieutenant governors of the various provinces may wish to have at their receptions are quite out of order. Furthermore, we cannot refer in this house to actions of lieutenant governors or matters affecting provincial legislatures.

Mr. Chairman, if I may raise a point of order, I quite agree with and I am not protesting what Your Honour has said about lieutenant governors and the Governor General, but surely when because of his race the hon. member for Skeena referred to a person who happens to be in the other place he was simply illustrating a point with respect to Indians, and was not discussing that gentleman's conduct in the other place or any speech he has made or anything he has done as a member of the other place. He was discussing the fact that an Indian was a member of the other place and was subject to additional embarrassment for that reason. It seems to me that it would be very restrictive indeed to our liberties in discussing the administration of the Indian Act if Your Honour were to insist upon so narrow an interpretation.
The government is very touchy on this subject.

As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, it is not my intention to embarrass anyone but merely to attempt to show the foolishness of our liquor laws as they apply to some people in Canada. However, I can say that a few years ago I deliberately invited a native Indian into my home, an Indian who was a member of a band and prohibited by law from consuming liquor in any other place except a licensed beer parlour or cocktail bar. Incidentally, Indians cannot get into the cocktail bars because of the discriminatory attitude of their operators. I invited this Indian into my home and offered him a drink. I mentioned to the R.C.M.P. beforehand what I was going to do and I was told not to worry, that they would not do anything about it. That again shows the ridiculousness of our liquor legislation. All I am trying to point at this time is that the situation is screwy, and that some action should be taken immediately.
You were trying to get someone into trouble.

I was trying, my friend says, to get somebody in trouble; that is about the extent of his knowledge of this situation. I am here to point out the necessity for an attitude of equality toward the people of this country whether their skins be coloured the same as yours or differently; whether they happen to have been born of parents who were in this country many years before my parents were in this country, or under any other circumstance.
I point out that our attitude toward these people is not one of equality but one of discrimination. This is another phase of it, and the problem rests squarely on the shoulders of the province. I know the Indian Act has been amended, in effect, to remove as much as possible the jurisdiction of the minister with regard to the liquor question as it relates to Indians. This problem has been pushed where it belongs, under the jurisdiction of the various provincial governments. I am complaining that they are at fault in not working in the direction in which they should be working. There is one province, Ontario, which is far advanced in so far as the question of liquor is concerned, and I wish to heaven the other provinces would follow suit.

I was glad, Mr. Chairman, last week to hear the minister say that it is the government's intention to see that the Indian population receive greater consideration. I understand that the department

of Indian affairs is conducting an experimental program in Manitoba which has to do with the rehabilitation of Indians who have been disabled by tuberculosis. This is a very commendable beginning, but it should not be limited to Manitoba. We have similar cases in the district of Thunder bay. It seems to me that Indians who have spent several months or years in a sanatorium should be helped, no matter where they live.
I suggest that Fort William or Port Arthur could be considered as an ideal centre for the establishment of a rehabilitation centre in one of the lakehead hospitals, preferably in one of the wings of the Fort William district sanatorium. Young men and women could be trained as orderlies or nurses' aides. These Indians could be taught some trades to enable them to become useful citizens, and at the same time give them a feeling that they are part of the community and enjoying equality of treatment, which I believe should be the answer for all Indian problems.
Another great need is adequate recreational facilities. The problem of unemployment is greater for the Indians than for the rest of the population because of their isolation. This makes constructive recreational outlets doubly important, as the young people tend to drift around and get into trouble. A few years ago, as a result of the generosity of the president of Canadian National Railways and a few people in Fort William, a small building was made available for recreational purposes. This has helped to some extent. However, the lack of proper direction and adequate assistance has limited its usefulness. Here is a place where the government can really do something which would not cost a great deal.
It is rather regrettable, but the Indians still do not have the full benefit of all the services provided by the Ontario government that other people enjoy. An example of this may be found in the matter of mothers' allowances. I submit that while the public welfare authorities may be experiencing certain difficulties in extending their services to Indians, and while a certain amount of time will be required to achieve a smoothly functioning procedure, this should not prevent them from receiving the full benefit of all our welfare services.
At the present time when an Indian family is destitute the amount of assistance it receives from the department is much below that which would be required for even a minimum standard of subsistence. If the act were amended so that a reserve would be regarded as a municipality for such welfare purposes, with the department of Indian affairs assuming the responsibility together with the band and the province providing its usual 66968-9-1194
