During a recent visit to my constituency I attended a meeting of the local Indian band, which is the Ojibway tribe. Their chief, Frank Pelletier, welcomed me to their reservation school and outlined some of their needs and grievances. He felt that there was a need for higher education. He deplored the neglect in the past, but hoped that the coming generation might obtain an education which would enable the Indian to stand on his own feet in a competitive world.
The next most important need is housing. The Indians do not have the funds to decently house their growing population. Some houses which were constructed a few years ago were poorly built; they were too low; they sagged, and the doors and windows stuck. Here, surely, was a case of total indifference and a definite lack of good workmanship. They do not ask for ultra-modern buildings, but something good and solid.
These Indians certainly complained about not having a vote in federal elections. This indeed seems to be a paradox. They can vote for a provincial member but they are not allowed to vote for a federal member when, in reality, it is the federal government which has jurisdiction over their affairs.
The majority of the men are employed cutting pulpwood, but their limits are almost exhausted and within two or three years this source of livelihood will be gone unless the government provides some new limits. There are several islands in the district with good stands of timber which would be ideal for their purpose. Some time ago some individual from the department of Indian affairs made a survey, but nothing has been heard of the outcome. There seems to be a lack of co-operation, if not total neglect, on the part of the department of Indian affairs in Ottawa.
In so far as education is concerned, the elementary schools are well conducted and presided over by competent teachers. One of them, Mrs. Mary Duggan, attended the meeting. She made the suggestion that in order to prepare pupils to absorb a higher education they should be given some vocational training, such as carpentry for the boys and sewing for the girls. The department should look into the matter, since it would not cost much to set up a couple of rooms in the basement of one of the schools and have someone supervise at least a limited vocational training program.
All the pupils capable of absorbing education wishing to attend high school in the city should be provided with transportation. A small bus or even a station wagon would

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration probably meet the requirements of those on the reservation. One father whose family lives in the reserve at Squaw bay, which is approximately seven miles from the nearest high school, has three children who wish to go to high school, but there is no means of transportation. That is just a case in point. Some 12 children do attend high school in the city, and they walk two miles to the nearest city bus line. Road conditions within the reservation are also poor and this matter came in for a lot of criticism from the gathering. Only $6,000 had been appropriated for road work in three reservations, which means that only a bit of patchwork on each can be expected.
The Fort William reservations own mount MacKay, which is about 900 feet above the level of lake Superior, at the back of which the Fort William watershed is located. That is a lake known as loch Lomond, which is seven miles long and about half a mile wide, from which lake our city gets its water. I might add that it is the purest water on the continent, flowing by gravity through a tunnel on the mountainside and piped to the city. It is so pure that it needs no distilling for any purpose. The purity and taste of this water have been favourably compared with the water flowing from the summit of mount Ben Nevis, which is the highest peak in the British isles, in Fort William, Scotland. There is a road leading up around the ledge of the mountain some 600 feet high, at the end of which there is a chapel and also a cross erected in memory of the Indian soldiers who fought and died in the first great war. This side of the mountain could be beautified, and with a good road would become one of the major tourist attractions of the lakehead. I believe the department should look into this feature as a means of revenue for the Indians of the local reserve.
Another question which is worthy of consideration is the status of the Indian in relation to our liquor laws. Our Indians are asking for the same privileges enjoyed by other people. It is rather a shame that an honest, civilized human being, because he is one of the original Canadians, upon entering a beverage room is faced with a large sign which reads, "Anyone caught serving an Indian will be prosecuted". Such is not the treatment that the forebears of our present Indians were promised when they all too trustingly agreed to let the white man take over most of their possessions. How can we speak of bills of rights when we are condoning such an injustice? In the event of war these men would be in the armed services. Many of them have served with distinction in both world wars, yet they are faced with the worst type of discrimination. Let us have

equal privileges for equal responsibilities. This glorious country of Canada cannot and should not have two classes of citizens. To quote the Indian chief of our tribe himself at this particular meeting, he said:
There is good and bad among all classes of men, but the majority of my people are law abiding and should be recognized as such.
Now I wish to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail in late February of 1959 and which contains a few paragraphs of an address delivered by Professor W. J. Morris of the University of Toronto:
Across the country, he said, Indians constitute the most economically depressed segment of our population. A once proud and noble people showed a high degree of co-operation toward the encroaching whites; and as their inheritance they are "tossed from municipal to provincial to dominion governments like the proverbial football".
He recalls that for decades there was a pitiful lack of educational facilities on reserves, and those that existed were furnished by the churches. These and welfare conditions have improved, but Indians forced off the reserves "by threat of starvation" find no comparable services among whites. For our 111,000 Eskimo, said Professor Morris, we spend more than twice as much as we do for 173,000 Indians. "This in itself is second class citizenship." And we need only recall recent testimony of Eskimo hardship to visualize the lot of the Indians.
With "our first real Indian act" dating only from 1951, Professor Morris says we have "operated on a hit and miss basis": and among his suggestions is research both economic and in the area of inter-personal relations, together with inter-government co-operation at all levels to utilize voluntary resources. "We have for long enough refused to accept any measure of responsibility as individuals for what is in effect the sorest blight on our Canadian conscience."
Those are important words. Two centuries of official bungling and evasion of a great human problem are in the last analysis a reproach on the monumental indifference of the Canadian people. It will in turn be their pressure which will give Indians their rightful heritage of first class citizenship.
As a matter of fact, the press of the country appears to be unanimous in its estimate of the situation. After 200 years since the royal proclamation, which said that no Indian could be dispossessed of his land without the crown's consent, this charter signed in 1763 being a guarantee of equality, these promises have not been fulfilled according to its terms.
I have a copy of another editorial which appeared in the Calgary Herald, which further illustrates, if more illustrations are needed, that the plight of the Indian is a question which concerns all Canadians. I quote:
Canadians are quick to offer advice and gratuitous opinions on racial problems in other countries. Yet Canadians are part of what might be called an unintentional conspiracy to keep the Indians as second class citizens. Canada's record with the native Indian population has some items of merit

to its credit over the years. Unfortunately we have only to look at the Indian population to realize that an entirely new approach is needed, and should be speeded to suit modern conditions.
Mr. Chairman, this is undoubtedly an accurate appraisal of the present status of our Indian population. I do not wish to cast any aspersions, or blame this or any former government. I simply express a belief and desire on the part of the great majority of the Canadian people that the time has arrived for the government of Canada to translate good intentions into a practical reality. I respectfully submit that the question of helping our Indian population is an urgent one and should be dealt with during this session of parliament.

First of all, may I say that I am wondering why the hon. member for Skeena spent so much of his time dealing with the question of liquor for Indians. I think the big problem which faces the Indian today is the opportunity to earn enough money to make a living so that in the long run he may have enough money left to buy his liquor after he gets his permit.
With regard to what he said about the difficulty experienced by an hon. member in the other place, I personally think that the hon. senator should apply for enfranchisement if he wants to drink liquor. All he needs to do under the terms of the Indian Act is to apply for enfranchisement.
I wish to express my appreciation today for the consideration which the minister has given to the question of destitute rations and to the problem of housing. In past years, as the hon. lady knows, I have been very critical of the meagre rations distributed to Indians who are destitute or who have returned to their homes from tuberculosis hospitals after being cured of T.B. The minister has given us the details with regard to destitute rations, and I wonder if she would be good enough, when she replies, to give us similar details with regard to rehabilitation rations, in particular those rations which are given to people who have returned from tuberculosis hospitals.
In each of the past five years the amount set aside in the estimates for providing Indians with housing, at least in my part of the country, has increased. However, I do not think it has increased at the rate it should have increased if we really intend to impress upon the Indians that we are conscientiously and seriously concerned about their living standards. I think we could well increase a great deal more those estimates, particularly where they concern the Northwest Territories.
I was happy to see that some attention has been paid to the economic development of

I wish also at this time to express my appreciation of the very fine work done by the officers of the hon. lady's department in my riding. In recent years we have found these officers coming into my riding in greater numbers, and we are thankful for that, and I am confident they are all very interested in the native people and anxious to bring about changes which would make it possible for Indians to realize a standard of living which could be compared, at least to some extent, with our own. I should like to make a suggestion to the minister with regard to the economic development of our Indian people.
As the minister knows, we have Indian agencies in the Northwest Territories at Yellowknife, at Smith, in Norman and Akla-vik, Hay River and Simpson. Each of these agents has to cover a very large area if they are to get into close contact with the natives and understand the problems of the communities over which they have jurisdiction. I wish to suggest to the minister that
the department should hire works foremen_____
let us call them that-in every settlement in the Northwest Territories where there is an Indian population. The duty of these work foremen would be to guide and give leadership to the Indian people in their economic

The people appointed should be men who know the conditions in the north, people who have lived in these communities, not someone who has just come out of the University of Toronto with a degree in welfare. The people I have in mind should be practical men who have lived with the Indians and who are interested in doing something to improve their conditions.
A further suggestion I have to make concerns co-operation between the Indians and the works foreman. I think any Indian agent would agree that in my part of the country, at least, the co-operation of the Indian chief of each particular band and settlement is very necessary if the government hopes to "sell" to the Indians a policy designed to raise their living standards and help them advance from their present static condition. But in the Northwest Territories they still have great influence over their people, and I suggest to the minister that her department should pay the chiefs some sort of salary for working in co-operation with the works foremen to which I have referred and helping to convince his people of the benefits of government policy in the field of economic development.
I also think that in every community there should be provided a tractor with a blade, a sawmill and a powered scow. I will go into this matter in somewhat more detail, pointing out what I think each of these pieces of equipment will or can do in order to help the Indian to place himself in a position where he can at least make a living like any other person in Canada.
At this time I would like to deal with the Great Slave lake area in particular. There are many communities centred around this lake including Yellowknife, Rae, Hay River, Fort Resolution, Rocher River and Snowdrift. Great Slave lake is considered to be the world's greatest source of whitefish and trout but on this lake you see only a handful of Indians working in the industry of commercial fishing. In my opinion many more of these people could be employed in this industry but you cannot say to an Indian, "Here you have this lake; the fish buyers are here so go out and fish." Any commercial fisherman must have a considerable amount of equipment. I suggest to the department that it should set up some sort of loan fund for Indians all around the lake including those people at Fort Providence and Fort Simpson who every fall go up the Mackenzie river into the lake to do their domestic fishing under


which a loan plan could be established. In other words these people could borrow money to equip themselves under the guidance of the works foreman to whom I previously made reference and establish themselves in the profitable business of commercial fishing on Great Slave lake.
Another thing that would be of assistance would be to have the department request the Department of Fisheries to conduct surveys to investigate the various inland lakes such as Lac la Marte to establish whether or not they are suitable for commercial fishing. If, for instance, Lac la Marte was found to be suitable for this purpose a number of our Indian people in the area around Rae, Lac la Marte and Hislop lake could be profitably employed in commercial fishing. I urge the department to take some steps toward supplying these people with guidance and equipment to encourage them to become engaged in useful projects of this type.
A few moments ago I said that every settlement in the district should be supplied with a tractor and other equipment. I appreciate that the first question that will be asked is: What will the Indians do with this equipment? In the Northwest Territories we have vocational training schools. Here the Indians are trained as operators of tractors and other equipment. These trained operators could be used during the early winter before the snow became too deep in hauling out logs cut by other Indians in the bush to supply the people in the area with material for proper housing for themselves. At the present time they tend to construct clapboard or plywood homes under a contract basis. I believe the Indians should be encouraged to haul out their own logs from the bush and build suitable homes for themselves.
The sawmill could square the logs and it could be operated by our native people under direction and guidance. There is no reason why one or two Indians from each settlement could not be trained in sawmill work at the vocational schools.
I also urge that a powered scow be provided at each settlement. Any person who has lived among Indians or dealt with them is aware that when winter comes they are faced with the problem of heating their homes. These people usually live for today with no real thought for tomorrow or the future and so their homes are heated from day to day as it were. If a scow were provided it could mean that those Indians who were unable to obtain salaried employment during the summer months could work in the bush cutting wood and transporting it to the settlements to provide themselves with a supply of firewood for the winter, and also

they could sell wood to those Indians who were gainfully employed on a payroll.
There are other things that could be done. Possibly some land clearing equipment could be provided in areas where there is land suitable for growing vegetables. The men could work the equipment and the women could look after the seeding and weeding and assist with the crops.
At this point I cannot resist telling the committee about a trip I took down the Mackenzie river in 1954 with the then minister of northern affairs and national resources. It was his first trip north after his appointment and of course at every place we visited the civil servants shined up the brass and showed us all the nice things in the north. We eventually arrived at Fort McPherson and were given a wonderful dinner. When we left the dining room the local school teacher invited the minister, the deputy minister and others including myself to see the garden project. We discovered six or seven Indian women pulling weeds in the garden. By the time we arrived there only half the garden had been weeded. The word had gone around that the minister was coming and the garden should be cleaned up quickly and although they had started at it in the morning they had not completed it by the time we arrived. If we had arrived in the morning before the warning had gone out we would have seen nothing but weeds in the garden.
There are, however, Indians in the north who have initiative and who are interested in working. They tell me that garden projects of this kind operated on a community basis is for the birds. They explained that some of them work very hard all summer in the garden and when the fall comes the crop is taken off and shared with the whole community. They said they would rather see the government split up these garden plots into individual acreage. They prefer to work their own plots and take off the produce that is the fruit of their individual labour.
That was a C.C.F. policy.

An hon. member comments that communal gardens were a C.C.F. policy and I agree. I have explained what has been happening under that policy. I hope the department will change its tune on that score and give these people some opportunity for individualism, a goal to work for and a degree of personal initiative.
I have dealt with some of the things we could do to improve the lot of the Indian people. It must be pointed out, however, that the fur industry is still the backbone of the economy of the native people in the Northwest

I appeal to the minister and ask her to see her friend, the Minister of Agriculture, and ask him why we cannot bring fur under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Everything else that is produced in this country can come under the act. At Fort Smith we are building government houses for civil servants and offices for civil servants. Most of the building that is going on is for civil servants and some Indians are working on those projects. Those construction programs will be over and finished in two years. Ever since we started that construction program I have repeatedly said that we had to look to the future. It is fine and dandy to have Indians on the payroll today and making a half decent living, but the minute that construction is over what are you going to do with the Indian? This is the problem and now is the time to start thinking about it. What are you going to do with the children who are coming out of the vocational training schools that we have built in all parts of the country. This is a problem that requires serious consideration now.
I noticed the minister said we will have placement officers. Have we one in the Northwest Territories? If we have, has any thought been given to what the placement officer is going to do to place Indians if there is nothing for them to do? When native people who have been told, "you take a vocational training course and you will receive jobs", find themselves out of work during the construction season and find, as I said a moment ago, carloads and aeroplane loads of men being shipped into the north to do jobs they could do, how do you think they feel about it?

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter coming under this vote upon which I should like to make a few comments. It is one which has not been discussed so far and I admit that it is somewhat complicated. Nonetheless, I hope that the minister will be able to give the committee some information about it. May I say first of all that I am raising this matter at the request of the president of the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood.
We all recognize that property and civil rights and natural resources come within the jurisdiction of the provinces while Indian affairs come within the jurisdiction of the federal government. However, it has been mentioned to me on a number of occasions and again recently by the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood that they would like to have a clear exposition from the minister as to how far she feels her responsibility extends in the conduct and direction of Indian affairs having regard to ownership of property and Indian rights within the boundaries of provinces, particularly where no treaty rights are involved.
We all recognize that the minister is faced with problems right now involving the Six Nations Indians and it may be on a somewhat similar basis that I have been asked to raise this matter in the committee at this time. I have been told on many occasions by Indian chiefs in British Columbia that they have never given over their ownership of British Columbia because there is no treaty under which they did so. However, I am not going into that phase of the matter this afternoon.
May I say that I am quite proud that the native Indians of British Columbia should take such interest in whether or not they hold ownership to lands and certain rights in respect of timber or minerals. In recent years they have expressed great interest in the development of the province and great interest particularly in the last year as to who will develop the province. They are primarily interested in the northern part of British Columbia where, as the minister knows, approximately one-fifth of the territory of British Columbia apparently is to be ceded by the Social Credit government of our province to a corporation or group of corporations nominally headed by Axel Wenner-Gren but behind whom we know are the Krupp interests of Germany. The Indians are concerned as to their status in the development of that part of the province under that type of ownership. I believe that the Indians of British Columbia generally

and the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood are to be congratulated, complimented and commended because of their interest in this matter. Perhaps the best way I can present the matter to the minister and the officers of her department is by doing what I was requested to do by the president of the grand council. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I will read the letter I received under date of February 20 on the official letterhead of the brotherhood. It reads in part as follows:
By the provision of section 109 of the B.N.A. Act, the title to the minerals and soil in a province is in the crown, the province and the Indians. Lord Watson in giving judgment for the privy council in the St. Catharines Milling case ruled in part as folows: "There is a third interest, and that interest is the Indian interest, which is capable of being vindicated in competition with the provincial interest."
By that fact and by law, as fortified by the privy council judgment. .. the B.C. Indians have an interest equal to the province but wacky Bennett has not consulted us in giving a big portion of what belongs to us Indians to Axel Wenner-Gren. The reason for this letter is to ask you to speak for us in the House of Commons and ask what kind of a man is this Axel Wenner-Gren? Is he worthy of a man to be allowed into British Columbia? The people of B.C. who are co-owners of what Bennett is going to give him... from the grapevine and the moccasin telegraph this Indian has been told by white people that Wenner-Gren made his millions dealing with human lives.
I say that that statement, Mr. Chairman, is a correct one. I continue:
That during world war II he dealt with the enemy, while also doing business with the allies.
That too is a correct statement, Mr. Chairman. I continue:
Is this gangster, who is worse than Capone, the kind of a man to do business with? What comes after this donation by Bennett may be detrimental to all the people in B.C. We may be enslaved, we must protect our posterity.
This comes from the Indian brotherhood in the interests of British Columbia, their own land. The letter continues:
You can use my name in these allegations because as the chosen leader of my people it is my duty to know and can only find this out through your questions in the parliament of Canada. The query must be directed to all hon. members of the House of Commons, not only the government, because they are the trustees for the Indians of Canada-The land that he is to get is rich in minerals, etc., and will adversely affect the economy of the Indians in that part.
I was asked to raise the matter in the house. That is signed by Andy Pauli, grand chief and president of the North American Indian brotherhood.
I felt it was my responsibility, Mr. Chairman, having received the letter to read it. As I previously stated, it is something to be proud of that our truly native-born Canadian citizens, our native Indians, are concerned
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration about the development of our natural resources, and who develop them. Basically their question is, what power, what influence, what interest has the minister in charge of Indian affairs at this time, to assist them in a situation in which British Columbia is making a deal with a man who, by order in council, was declared a traitor and a person with whom no one could deal during the last war.
I was so interested in the letter and in the other statements made that I checked on the St. Catharines Milling and Lumber Company case, a decision of the privy council, which is to be found in Canadian Constitutional Decisions of the Judicial Committee by Olmsted. I am not going to go into the decision in detail, but I did find some interesting facts in that judgment of the privy council. May I just give a couple of quotations which I feel are important. On page 238, the judgment says:
Documentary evidence was referred to, to show the nature and character of the Indian title. It was contended that the effect of it was to show that from the earliest times the Indians had, and were always recognized as having, a complete proprietary interest, limited by an imperfect power of alienation.
On page 241, we find this:
It is contrary to the spirit of the act to hold that the grant of legislative power-
That is the British North America Act.
-over lands reserved for the Indians carries with it by implication a grant of proprietary right.
I am not going to continue with that, but I do believe sincerely that the North American Indian brotherhood has raised a most interesting, if complicated, question. I do hope that the minister may find it possible, because of her interest in the department over which she exercises jurisdiction, to take note of the situation in British Columbia and the interest of the native Indians of British Columbia in their own proprietary right to develop the resources of the province, who develops them, and perhaps inform the native brotherhood through the medium of what she says in this house as to what their position is and what help they can expect in defending, not only their own hunting and fishing grounds but the natural resources, thereby honouring their ancestors who were the original settlers of that great province.

I have two or three questions to ask the minister which I have been directed to ask by some people in Ottawa. Are there any solicitors employed by the department in connection with Indian affairs? If so, what are their salaries and have they passed the necessary examinations to qualify as solicitors in any province of Canada?

There are a few questions I should like to put to the minister before she replies. I do not intend to make a speech, and I am sure she will be relieved to hear that. I think we would all be interested in the most up to date information she has about what is going on on the Six Nations reserve. It did happen, I think it was last night or at any rate very recently, that I was looking at television which I do not very often do. I saw the superintendent of the Six Nations reserve on television. He expressed the view- I am not taking any exception to this or anything of that sort-that the sooner we found out what the people of that reserve really wanted, the better.
As a matter of fact, this had already occurred to me even before I saw this television program. I thought perhaps it would be advisable-I am only putting this forward very tentatively because I think the minister appreciates I have no desire to make any difficulties at all in connection with this matter-to have a plebiscite on the reserve to ascertain whether or not the majority of the Indians want to continue to have an elective council or want to have the restoration of the government of the so-called hereditary chiefs. I know there would be considerable difficulties if the second course happened to be the wish of the people because of the claims that are made by the hereditary chiefs that they are not Canadian citizens and the reserve is not a part of Canada but an independent country.
I have to confess that I do not know whether or not this course has ever been taken or ever been considered. It may be that at one time a decision was made by the courts on this matter. I understand that there was a certain treaty in the time of Sir Frederick Haldimand which had a good deal to do with the status of the reserve and of the Indians living on the reserve. I am wondering if possibly it might be a good idea, by agreement if agreement can be secured, to refer that document and any of the other relevant documents to the supreme court, with a view to getting an authoritative interpretation of them. I imagine there would not be much purpose to be served in doing that unless there was a prior agreement with the parties interested that they would accept an interpretation by the supreme court. It might be impossible to obtain such an agreement.
These two ideas had crossed my mind, and I thought, it would be useful to put them forward. I do not expect the hon. lady to make any particular comment about them. However, I would appreciate it, and I think other members of the committee would, in


view of some of the things that have been happening, if without taking too much time we could be told as much as the hon. lady has in the way of information as to what is occurring.
I am also very much interested in being brought up to date, as I am sure would be other hon. members of the committee, about the progress of the famous expropriations at Caughnawaga. I have spent a good deal of time on, and given a good deal of attention to, this subject, and I am sure the hon. lady has done the same and I would again like to know what the current situation is. While I am not seeking to go underground or anything like that, I would also like to hear a little more about water mains and the sewers, and how they are coming along at Caughnawaga.

I told you all I knew
the other day.

I thought I gave a pretty
full answer, but I will see if there is any more information.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to ask the minister a question about a matter which has arisen on the Indian reserve at Gleichen. The situation there is one of concern as regards the financial difficulty of the Indians on that reserve. A situation has arisen whereby the Indians, who for a number of years have farmed their own land and built up a capital reserve, now find that that capital reserve has diminished and that they are in such financial difficulty that they are unable to farm their own land. Also, consideration is being given to renting that land to the white man. This is a sort of reflection on the administration of that Indian reserve, either through the failure to have farm management men there to assist and supervise the Indians in the proper management of their land, or it could be due to a number of other causes. Nevertheless, the fact remains that the Indians on that reserve now find it necessary to seek jobs off the reserve in order to gain a livelihood. It seems to me that the Indian affairs branch should, in their wisdom and administration of the affairs of that reserve, give careful consideration, if they have not already done so, to the step which is now contemplated.
That land belongs to the Indians, and I submit that before it is leased to the white man and before long term contracts and commitments are made, the Indians' fundamental problems should be probed to the very depths in order to see if by financial help or other arrangement something cannot be done by this government to bring about a situation on that reserve where these Indians can profitably administer and farm their own land.

I wonder if I might briefly pose a couple of questions to the minister. I understand that we make a grant to the national commission on the Indian Canadians. I would like to know how much that is. I cannot find any reference to it in the details, but it is the amount of the grant we make which I want.
You will find it under the citizenship branch.
Is it listed as an amount?
No, it is not. I will find it for you.

Thank you. My other question is this. On October 30 and 31, 1958 there was a provincial conference of Saskatchewan Indian chiefs and councillors held at Fort Qu'Appelle. I would like to take the liberty, if I may, of reading one of the resolutions passed at that conference. One reads:
We, the chiefs and councillors of the association of Saskatchewan Indians, in conference assembled,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration request the federal government to undertake a detailed social survey of Saskatchewan Indians to among other things
(1)	gather factual information on the conditions prevailing on all reservations;
(2)	make recommendations as to policies and programs designed to provide for the advancement and improvement of Saskatchewan Indians, and
(3)	determine the most effective methods of implementing these programs.
I wonder if the minister would indicate whether the association of Indian chiefs has officially communicated the contents of this resolution, or the import of it, to the minister, and what action has been taken or is contemplated with respect to the suggestions made therein?

Mr. Chairman, possibly I could try to answer now some of the questions which have been put in the course of this debate. In so doing, may I thank the hon. members for their interest and say to them that all of the constructive suggestions which have been made will certainly be dealt with by this department, and consideration will be given to them. There are two or three very good suggestions which have come out of the debate today. I might say further that the officials of my department are ready and willing at all times to consult with members who wish to bring to them suggestions, or who wish clarification of existing conditions on any of the reserves.
With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena, perhaps I should answer his last reference first. The resolution from the conference at Fort Qu'Appelle was forwarded to the branch and we have it. There are certain difficulties in the way of proceeding immediately; the matter is under consideration. I might tell him that it took five years from the time of the first consideration of the report now known as the Hawthorn report on the British Columbia Indians before the study was finally undertaken. These things cannot be done overnight. If my memory serves me well it is now something in the nature of two years since the suggestion was first made that a similar study, or something approximating the same kind of study, be made amongst the Indians in Saskatchewan. We are considering the matter. It is the opinion of those who have studied the Hawthorn report that much of the material in that report is of general interest to Indians right across Canada, and we do not wish to duplicate the work which was put into that report. I can assure the hon. member that the matter is under study at the present time. Eventually there will be a study made, but that will depend upon the speed with which we can arrive at terms of reference establishing such a study.

I noted what the hon. member had to say with reference to relief payments. I am sure he will agree with me that the schedule now established represents a great improvement over that formerly in effect. I cannot let this opportunity pass without commenting on the fact that last year when this subject was under discussion I maintained, from the available figures, that the average relief payment made was around $14. The hon. member maintained it was $10, and the press of this country picked up that amount and made it known that the amount of relief payments to Indians was $10, despite the fact that I had given a different figure. This year, however, when payments have been increased to a minimum of $22 for the first single adult, the hon. member indicates that this represents a very small increase. comes under provincial jurisdiction. Does this provision that the initiative must rest with the Indians themselves form part of the Indian Act?
No. The request must come from the province, but the province naturally does not move until it is sure of what the Indians want.

Since the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has returned, perhaps I might deal with some of the matters he raised. I should like to refer first of all to the situation at the Six Nations reserves. Possibly I had better tell the house what has already become public knowledge since it happened last night after the house rose.
Yesterday on the Six Nations reserve the new Iroquois police, as they style themselves, arrested one of our school teachers, an Indian by the name of George Beaver. They charged him with treason because he had written a letter to a local newspaper criticizing the action of the hereditary chiefs. They incarcerated him in the basement of the council house where they kept him for some time. They finally tried him for treason. I understand they found him guilty and then released him with a warning not to do it again. However, Mr. Chairman, it is my opinion that we must protect Canadian citizens and accordingly I should like to read into the record the telegram which I sent to Joseph Logan, Sr. who has been speaking for the hereditary chiefs. It reads as follows:
Joseph Logan, Esq.,
Ohsweken,
Ontario.
It has been brought to my attention that citizens have been molested and detained by an alleged Indian police force on the Six Nations reserve said to be under the direction of your organization. I am further informed that some of these persons have been subjected to mock trials and in some instances ordered to pay fines.
This type of conduct cannot be tolerated and I must most emphatically advise all those members of the Six Nations participating in and who are responsible for such unlawful conduct that it must cease immediately.
I must further inform you that steps will be taken without delay to restore and maintain peace and order on the Six Nations reserve for the protection and quiet enjoyment of all citizens.
The telegram is signed by the minister. I am not sure whether the hon. member made a suggestion or was thinking out loud, but with respect to his remarks about the proposed plebiscite I may say that is something that has occurred to some of the members of my staff. We have been discussing the matter. I think little would be achieved by proceeding in the heat of the present situation but I draw to his attention also that in any event nothing can be done at the moment because the authority of the hereditary chiefs is being argued at the present


time before the courts in Ontario. Until that matter is settled I think we would be wrong in taking any action.

I wonder whether the hon. lady would allow me to interrupt her for the purpose of obtaining information. How did that case get there? I do not want to say anything about the case but how did it get before the courts? Is my memory failing or is it something that occurred since the hon. lady became minister?

I think it was already started when I came into the department. As I understand the situation, and my officials will correct me if I am wrong, the hereditary chiefs challenged the action of the elected council with regard to the sale of a piece of property.
That would have been after my time.

The matter is now before the courts and, of course, we must await the outcome. The hon. member also asked me a question with reference to Caughnawaga. The area expropriated was 1,374.14 acres. The number of individuals entitled to compensation was 217. As of February 24, 1959, settlement has been completed with 198 of them or some 91 per cent and settlements are pending with the other 19. The total amount of compensation paid to individuals as of February 24, 1959, was $2,217,892.20.
Have any of these cases gone into the courts?

No, there are none in the courts. I said in the absence of the hon. gentleman that I thought that the rest of his questions had to do with education. Would he like to wait until we reach the education item?

I would be quite happy to wait until that time. However, another question has been put to me. Perhaps it is a little unfair of me to ask the hon. lady without trying to find out for myself but as she has so much more research staff than I have perhaps she will not mind. It has been represented to me by some Caughnawaga Indians that they are very fearful of this proposed metropolitan Montreal arrangement. They feel Mr. Duplessis is attacking the autonomy of the Caughnawaga reserve. I wonder if the hon. lady knows whether the reserve is to be included in the metropolitan area or definitely excluded?
I can assure the hon. gentleman I have made no changes in the law. As he knows, under the present situation no one can encroach on a reserve, so the Indians are quite safe.

It occurred to me it would, of course, be quite incompetent for the provincial legislature to attempt to legislate a reserve into part of a municipality. I did not think there could be anything in this, but I thought there would not be any harm in asking the question since it had been put to me.
No, not at all. As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me well, we did have some correspondence with at least some members of the band in that regard, and gave them that answer.

There is another question about Caughnawaga, and that is the question of re-routing the road and re-routing the bridge. Have all problems of that sort been settled with the provincial authorities and with the Indians?

I do not know that they have been settled. The Indians have objected to any change in the road and so long as their objection stands nothing will be done about it. Unless they can come to an agreement, nothing will be done. I believe that some of the provincial authorities wanted to discuss the matter with them, but they were not even amenable to that suggestion so the department does not intend to take any action on the matter so long as the opinion of the Indians is that they want no change.
There were also some expropriations at St. Regis. Have they all been settled?
The area of the reserve expropriated was 140.3 acres; the number of individuals entitled to compensation, 40. All of the settlements have been completed and the total compensation paid was $184,771.
Well, that is a happy ending.

I have one very minor question before this item passes. It relates not only to this particular vote, but to every other vote in the book. At the last session I urged that something be done about this, and if I could indicate it to the minister now perhaps she could communicate with the authorities responsible for the compilation of the statistical information in the estimates book. What I am suggesting is this: in the second portion of the book containing the details of the services, would it not be possible to arrange to print in that section the number of the vote, just as it is in the front of the book? We find great difficulty in following exactly what vote we are dealing with in the detailed section.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I wondered if I raised the question at this session, perhaps next session and eventually we will be able to have the vote number printed in the detailed sections of the book.
If the hon. member will mention it to the Minister of Finance when his estimates are before the committee, he will be putting it to the proper authority.
Will the hon. lady join me?
I shall be glad to.

The hon. lady will remember that there was a good deal of debate and a good deal of agitation at one time about the completion of the band lists, particularly in relation to certain happenings in Alberta that were ultimately settled in the courts, as they should have been in the first place. There were, the last time I made inquiries, still a few cases pending and I just wondered if the hon. lady could bring us up to date, and let us know if that job is also completed?
It is practically completed, Mr. Chairman. The protests remaining are down to two, and we hope that these will be handled to their satisfaction shortly.
Are these two persons living on the reserve or not living on the reserve? I would be interested in their history. Perhaps I could find a grievance.
The reason they have not been settled is that we cannot locate them.

Item agreed to.
Indian agencies-
57. Operation and maintenance. $3,728,028.

In connection with this item, page 144, there is an item about three-quarters of the way down the page, listed as allowances. There is quite a substantial increase in the vote, from $40,000 to $100,000. Would the minister give us information on that?
This results from the revised scale of northern allowances.

I believe the hon. member for Mackenzie River wanted to ask a question, although he does not seem to be in the committee at the moment. He wanted to ask about northern allowances to ascertain whether they were on precisely the same scale in Indian affairs as they are in northern affairs.
Yes, they are precisely the same.

Item agreed to.
1888	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Reserves and trusts-
59. Operation and maintenance, $367,421.

This is an old favourite of mine, as the minister well knows. Perhaps the minister would like to leave this until we resume at eight o'clock, when she could tell us just where these estates stand. It is one of the most vexing problems, as I found when I was in the department, and I am sure a lot of us hope the situation is improving steadily. I should like to have a fairly detailed report on what the situation is.

I think with all the information I have at hand I can manage to give it to the committee before six o'clock. The estates which were concluded in 1956-57 were 1,420; in 1957-58, 1,179; 1958-59-this is just from April to December-the last figure I have is 2,412. Now, in the management of estates opened, in the 1956-57 year we find they were 667; in 1957-58, 702; and in 1958-59, for the same period April to December 31, 508.
Has the hon. lady the global figure for the backlog at present?
My officials do not have the figures for the backlog at present.
I think there are a couple of other questions I should like to ask, so perhaps we could let this stand.
From the information I gave, the hon. member will realize we are cutting steadily into the backlog.
I think it is very encouraging.

How far we have gone, I could not say at the moment, but I shall try to find out.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We have been discussing item No. 59. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to address a few remarks on the first item before it carries. There are a number of items which are of some concern to the Indian people of the Yukon. I want particularly to draw to the hon. minister's attention matters concerning housing, children's aid, welfare payments in isolated areas, education, both schools and hostels, and land. Perhaps I could first refer to the minutes of a meeting held in Whitehorse between the


superintendent of the Yukon agency and five members of the legislative council of the Yukon, as well as Commissioner Collins. At that meeting the main topic of discussion was the matter of welfare payments to Indian people in isolated areas. The following resolution was passed:
Be it resolved, in order that the economic welfare of Old Crow, Ross river and such other areas as may be found necessary at a later date, be better secured, it is desirable to pay to each adult Indian or person living the Indian mode of life, who kills a wolf by means other than poisoning and delivers the pelt to the R.C.M.P., the sum of twenty dollars as a rehabilitation measure for an experimental period of not more than three years. The pelt to remain the property of the person killing the animal.
This matter of welfare I have already discussed with the director of the branch, who has been very helpful and who has given me reason to believe that some sympathy, perhaps, exists in the branch for the people of these rather remote areas, and that they may expect some assistance in this regard.
Another subject which was discussed at this same meeting was the matter of the allotment of land. I would like to call to the attention of the minister the fact that the five members of the legislative council of the Yukon were present at this meeting and all these resolutions were passed unanimously, with the exception of the one concerning the re-establishment of the bounty, and that received unanimous consent with the exception of one voice. This resolution concerning land was passed:
Be it resolved that inasmuch as no treaty exists between the Indians of the Yukon, and the government of Canada, it would seem desirable, with the consent of the Indians of the Yukon, to make some arrangements regarding individual and band land allotments at this time as a measure of security.
This matter of the allotment of land to the Indian people of the Yukon is one which should be of some concern to the minister, as I am sure it is. The time has come when some arrangement has to be made for the Indian people of the Yukon. If it is not the intention of the department to allot tracts of land, which was the normal course followed in other parts of Canada, may I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to setting up band council funds in lieu thereof.
The territorial council at its last session considered these matters, and I have before me a copy of the votes and proceedings of the legislative council which was prepared last year. In debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, Councillor George Shaw of Dawson said this:
Another matter, Mr. Speaker, that I feel strongly about, is the matter of extermination of predatory

animals, more specifically the wolf. I can quite understand how nature balances the continuity of the different species of animals; however, I do not think that nature always takes into account, in its balancing, the effect that man has created in his need of game animals, either for meat or sport. Accordingly, statistics have proven that caribou are very much decreasing in number; the people who feel the impact of this most severely are the Indian population that subsist primarily on these animals for food and clothing, etc. To assist these people, whose very lives depend on these large herds continuing, I consider it imperative that a bounty be placed on wolves. Such an action without question will substantially deplete the wolves in the area concerned; also will assist the Indian trappers in what is now a most depressed industry.
These remarks of Councillor Shaw may be used to point out the present need for consideration being given to the resolution which was passed at the meeting of December 29, 1958, at Whitehorse. Councillor Shaw brought up another matter at the last session of the legislative council when he discussed the education of young Indian people. In this same debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, he says:
It is commendable, and I welcome the government's plan, to provide vocational training to the younger Indians; however, it is still necessary that the older members be taken into consideration and assisted in a manner by which they can maintain their self-respect in a type of livelihood with which they are acquainted.
Since the hon. minister assumed office she has caused action to be taken for the construction of a new school at Old Crow. This is extremely commendable. The school is being constructed not only with native materials but with native labour. This will put substantial numbers of breadwinners into this area to work; work which is vitally required at this particular time of the year in view of the fact that in the last year and a half the fur industry has dropped to a new low, thereby severely restricting the range of income which these people have at their disposal. This type of program is recommended for other such projects which are required in other like areas, but in the meantime it is necessary to consider the remoter areas, such as Ross river, and consider the feasibility of following the advice of the legislative council of the Yukon, as well as the commissioner-I may add my own opinion to that-regarding the implementation of these welfare payments in the form of wolf bounties in the remoter areas. This is a new approach to the matter of a wolf bounty. It is not a question of a handout but of a monetary payment in the form of a welfare grant which, at the same time, assists in the control of predatory animals.
I pass on quickly to the matter of children's aid. I believe the hon. minister was presented with a brief by the Southern Yukon
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Children's Aid Society. This is an organization which was formed recently. When I say recently, I should say in the last three or four years. This organization has done more to alleviate suffering and hardship among the infant population in the Yukon than any other organization of which I am aware. This is an organization which until now has been entirely supported by private subscription; that is to say, it has had no connection with the government. A surprising fact is that 74.6 per cent of the cases that were handled by this society during the period January, 1958 to October, 1958 were cases involving Indian children, Indians of white status or halfbreeds. At the moment this organization is gaining support only by private subscription. The brief which was presented by the children's aid society asked for government financial help. I think, Mr. Chairman, this is a matter which deserves the very special consideration of the minister. I simply quote the last paragraph of the brief which was presented in order to show the need for the immediate consideration of the request made by this organization. It reads:
Though we have never previously requested financial aid from the department, the society now has to request an annual grant, despite generous contributions from the public. Our work has increased four-fold, necessitating additional paid help, rental of an office, and many other expenses. Our whole program is expanding and we will need more financial support from the departments of the government we are serving. The amount we are asking is $3,000 annually. A brief has been submitted to the territorial government requesting an increase in our annual grant, and if we fail in our efforts to obtain these, our treasurer reports that we shall be forced to cease to function after May 1959.
I commend this request to the minister's special consideration, because without such aid the society, as it has said, will be forced to discontinue this work. I know that the minister and all hon. members will agree that this is an effort that is deserving of every possible support.
I should like to conclude my remarks by referring to the minutes of a conference of Indian delegates which was held at Whitehorse on June 10, 1958. I believe the director of the branch, who has done such wonderful work in the Yukon in the last two years, was in attendance at that meeting. The Indian delegates who represented their various bands at this meeting brought up matters ranging from housing, education and aid to trappers, to bounties and refrigeration. In fact, the whole field of Indian affairs was covered. Two or three of the outstanding features of the ensuing brief deserve particular consideration.
One refers to the fact that unemployment insurance is not now available to two classes

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of Indian people in the Yukon, and I assume this also applies elsewhere. The first class of people affected are Indian trappers, and the second are those engaged in forest firefighting duties. The Indian people feel that unemployment insurance should be paid to Indian people who are engaged in trapping and firefighting on the same basis as it is paid to those engaged in fishing. They believe that when trappers or firefighters are out of work they are entitled to receive unemployment insurance.
There is one further matter which is of some importance and which I should like to include as having been among the subjects dealt with, at the meeting on December 29, by the legislators of the territorial council. This concerns the need for an Indian placement officer, and a recommendation to this effect was unanimously supported at that meeting. Again I say that this represents the view of the Commissioner of the territory and of the five members of the Legislative Council of the Yukon, in addition to the heads of the two main branches of the church up there, and many other people. Bishop Coudert who is the bishop of the Roman Catholic church in the Yukon, said specifically that there is a need for a placement officer in the Yukon agency. This particular request was also made by the various Indian people who made up the delegation which attended the meeting last July. Bishop Coudert also stated that there is a need for the Indians and halfbreeds in the Whitehorse area to be provided with additional houses. I know that the minister is making progress in this regard, and I should like to commend her on this work.
Bishop Greenwood of the Anglican church reiterated the need for an Indian placement officer. He said, further, that the care of old and disabled Indian people presented a problem. He also expressed the feeling that steps should be taken in order to permit the inclusion in the bands of some illegitimate children of Indian women born between September 1951 and August 1956 in addition to legally adopted children. This is very important because unless these people are classified as Indians they cannot attend the schools set up specifically for Indian children; they are neither white nor Indian as far as the definition given in the Indian Act is concerned. Unless they fall within the definition given in the act they are denied the right of access to the Indian schools. They are also being denied the right of access to the hostels which are being constructed at the moment in Whitehorse, so

they cannot come into Whitehorse from outlying points and attend the new schools, because they have no place in which to live.
There is a very pressing need for something to be done about this situation. It is something which requires immediate attention. I think this view has been expressed by Commissioner Collins and by others in the Yukon and I would suggest that the minister give this matter every consideration prior to the opening of these new hostels and the school in Whitehorse, because otherwise these children would be denied the educational facilities which are being provided.
One further thing which came out of this meeting last June at which the director was in attendance was a statement by an Indian delegate that more liaison work could be done with regard to the integration of the Indian people into jobs in industry. This, once again, emphasizes the need for the establishment of an Indian placement officer in the Yukon. It seems odd that there should be more government employees concerned with the administration of forests and wild life in the Yukon than are concerned with the welfare of the Indian people. I trust the situation will not continue to be as it has been over the past 30 years.
With regard to the question of freezers there are, I believe, two freezers being built in the Yukon in different locations, but there is need for one in Dawson. Perhaps I could do no better here than quote from the remarks which were made last June at the conference which was held with the chief of the Dawson band. The latter said this absence of freezer facilities was a matter for regret. Apropos of this, an amusing story was told by Chief Charlie Mason. An Indian agent once had locker-freezers built in two places. One was not a place where a freezer was needed. An Indian from a place that needed a freezer locker said, "Why did you build one in that town?" The agent said, "I made a mistake". The Indian said, "I wish you would make a mistake and build one in our place." Dawson natives hope that soon a mistake will be made and a freezer put in Dawson for the native people commented Chief Mason.
I could do no better than conclude with the words of that chief as set out in these minutes:
It would seem that the native wants many things. It is true. He feels he has been robbed of his land and his livelihood and not much has been given in return. He feels that nobody cares much for his adjustment to the new way of life. Some people work and help but they have not the money or the time or the authority to do much. The native needs more understanding. We feel we should have an assistant agent living in Dawson who will be with us from day to day. The agent

could help us and teach us better and make us happier. Our people are getting more and more in number every year. The agent should be able to give us help now before the problems get too big.
Chief Mason continues:
Sometimes the agent says he is too busy in Whitehorse to come to Dawson. The department is like the candidate for parliament who visited Old Crow.
I may say that the chief is not speaking about me here, he is speaking about my then opponent.
He got off the plane. He said to the people "I am sorry I am late. For five days there was bad weather." One of the men said, "That is too bad. Did you have bad weather for the nine years before that?"
Mr. Jutras helps us out a lot and is thinking a great deal about us, but the head of his department should give him authority to put a man in Dawson. For too long the government has been away from us and has not come to help us. Mr. Meek was a good agent too, but he needed more help. So we think it is important to have an agent or representative for the agent in Dawson.
I thank you for listening to this our letter from Dawson natives. We hope that you will consider it with sympathy.
These are not isolated ideas, but are common and shared by all the Indian people of the Yukon. The problems have been stated before and I commend them to the minister for her sympathetic attention.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to what was said concerning the people at Old Crow by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat may I say that I am sure he knows these people come under the Indian agency which is in part of my riding and I am sure from now on they will looked after properly and very well.
Before the evening recess the minister replied to some of the suggestions I proposed early in the afternoon. I noted that she said there was some merit in the hiring of works foremen in the various settlements in the north. I wonder if the minister would give an opinion as to some of the other suggestions I made. In particular I should like to have her comments on my suggestion concerning the payment of salaries to Indian chiefs who would work in co-operation with the works foremen in selling government policy to the native Indians. I am sure the minister and the officials of the department realize how valuable it would be to have the co-operation of the chiefs in these settlements when projects are undertaken which are aimed at bringing the Indians out of their present condition into a better world.

Mr. Chairman, may I interrupt the hon. member. He raised the subject on the first item of this department, No. 56, and I did answer him at that time. True enough, I did not deal with every suggestion
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration he made but I suggest to him that he is now re-hashing an item which has been passed. All of the suggestions he made will be considered by the department.
At this moment, Mr. Chairman, I am uncertain whether we are considering item No. 59 or 60. I thought No. 59 was passed but it appeared to me that the hon. member for the Yukon was directing his remarks entirely to No. 60. Possibly we could straighten that out now.
I do not wish to disagree with the minister or with the Chair but I believe we are considering item No. 59 at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on item No. 59 at present.

If we are on No. 59, Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I thought we had passed that item but since we are still on it perhaps I could tell the hon. gentleman that we can only estimate the backlog of estates. About three years ago there were approximately 9,000 and it has now been reduced to approximately 5,000. I am expressing this in round figures, of course. The hon. gentleman will understand that it is a little difficult for us to arrive at an exact figure. To do so would require careful review of a large number of old estates. Sometimes when a new estate is opened it in turn reflects upon or has some bearing upon an old estate until a few matters are cleared up concerning the old estate, and so on. While not entirely satisfactory the figures show a rather remarkable improvement over the last three years, let us say.

The minister is quite
satisfied now that she has a good organization for dealing with this?
Yes.
When I was minister I often said I was thoroughly dissatisfied with the situation and I attempted to do a great deal to improve it. I am glad to hear it is working itself out.
I am sure the hon. member will understand that once you start to improve a thing it snowballs-
I am only too happy to take the credit, Mr. Chairman.
I might say it looks very encouraging now. We are on our way to cutting a large slice out of this backlog and I believe over a period of time it will eventually come down to a much smaller figure.

Item agreed to.
1892	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Welfare of Indians-
60. Operation and maintenance, $6,817,932.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that some of the questions I asked this afternoon relating to the welfare of Indians have not been answered and I wonder if the minister will consider this an appropriate item under which to comment on those matters?

Mr. Chairman, at six
o'clock I checked all my notes and I thought I had answered the hon. member in every respect except in a couple of instances where the hon. gentleman raised questions that obviously I could not answer off the cuff. It is necessary to have consultation with the department on some of these matters. I cannot give him an offhand answer on some of these issues. As far as I am aware I have answered every question he posed that could possibly be answered orally.
I wish now to say a few words with respect to the questions raised by the hon. member for the Yukon who made some serious suggestions. I might tell him the matter of unemployment insurance does not come under the jurisdiction of this department and he will have to raise his questions when the estimates of the Department of Labour are called. We are attempting to have placement officers stationed at all places where they may be usefully employed. We are gradually placing them in areas where they have not been placed heretofore and I hope we will get around to the Yukon shortly.
The matter of co-operation with the children's aid society is under active consideration and I think will come to a successful conclusion very shortly.
Is the hon. lady going to tell me about my cash relief, Mr. Chairman?
Mr. Chairman, I thought I had dealt with that question early in the afternoon. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would care to repeat his question.
If the hon. lady has dealt with it, I apologize. I was out of the chamber for a little while and she may have answered it during my absence.

Mr. Chairman, with all due deference may I say that I was present this afternoon and I cannot recall that the hon. lady commented on several of the suggestions I offered. I should like to have her comments on my proposal with regard to her department supplying to the Department of Transport a list of graduates from vocational training schools who could operate equipment for that and other departments on contract work. I should like to have her speak about my suggestion concerning the payment of a salary to Indian chiefs who 

would work as, shall I say, straw bosses or assistants to the works foremen. I do not recall that she gave an opinion with respect to my proposal about having the Department of Fisheries conduct surveys on inland lakes to see if they are suitable for commercial fishing by Indians. There was also the suggestion about providing equipment to assist Indians wishing to engage in commercial fishing on Great Slave lake and other related questions.

Mr. Chairman, with respect I submit that I did answer those questions in a general way. The hon. member knows that I cannot answer for other departments of government. I did tell him that every suggestion he made would be very carefully considered. Some of the suggestions he made I am sure he himself in all fairness would not expect me to answer immediately without consultation with my department and without full consideration of the implications of some of the rather drastic ones that he did make. As to some of the suggestions he made, I would ask him to give the department a chance to digest what he has asked and not press for an answer now because, in any event, I cannot give an answer particularly to problems which have interdepartmental implications.

Mr. Chairman, I will take for granted that the minister agreed with what I said. I personally did not think that some of the questions, particularly those in regard to employment by the Department of Transport in the filling of vacancies and so on, were answered but I will look forward to reading Hansard tomorrow to see what the minister did say in this respect.

Possibly I did not answer that particular one, but I can tell the hon. member that this department has circularized to all departments of government a plea to employ Indians wherever possible. We have met with considerable success in a great many parts of the country. I do not think any steps have yet been taken with regard to circularizing subcontractors but we are taking that into consideration. I can assure him that this department is pressing as hard as it can to employ Indians wherever possible in the areas in which they are resident.
I asked this afternoon whether a placement officer would be located in the Northwest Territories.
I answered that really when I was answering the hon. member for the Yukon. We are hopeful of placing officers in those various sections of the country as quickly as possible.

Item agreed to.

Economic development of Indians-
62. Operation and maintenance including an amount of $5,700 for grants to promote Indian agriculture, handicrafts and economic enterprises generally, $867,272.

The hon. lady knows exactly what I am going to ask her on this item. I want to know whether a successor has yet been appointed to Mr. Mel Jack, and whether she is satisfied with him and what is he doing?

Mr. Chairman, I am very sorry to say that there has been no successor appointed as yet. I am most regretful about that. We have held two competitions but, as the hon. member very well knows, this is a position which requires a peculiar kind of specialized background. He was fortunate enough to secure a man who had that kind of background. If he can suggest to me one who can take his place I can assure him that I will treat his suggestion with the greatest consideration because I would like to find someone right at the moment who could really do the job.

Mr. Chairman, I can suggest to the hon. lady that she could not do any better than to get Mr. Jack back. I do not know anybody in the country who is likely to do the job better than he did and I would certainly like to see him back there.
I can assure you that he will not be back.

He will be after a while, but not for two or three years. In the meantime, of course, the hon. lady has to get somebody else. I suggest that probably one of the difficulties is that it is very hard to convince the hon. lady's neighbour who sits in the chair next to hers that an adequate salary should be paid for the position.

I would not argue that point with the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, but I think we are agreed on one thing, namely that this is a most difficult post to fill. Now that the hon. member has been answered by the Minister of Transport I think he realizes what I am up against.
Quite; I understand.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the minister said that her department would continue, regardless of what the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was doing, their setup of industrial and economic welfare in the Northwest Territories. She did say at that time that the Indian affairs division could ask for and pay for services provided by other departments in the north. If she is considering the fact that the Indian affairs division will ask the Department of Northern Affairs and National 66968-9-120
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Resources to take over this responsibility of economic development of Indians in the Northwest Territories I would hope that she would make it very plain to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that we do not want any long-haired Ph.D.'s. Make it clear to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that we want practical men hired for these positions, men who will be looking after the welfare and the economic conditions of the Indians in the north, people who have lived with the Indians, know their conditions and are interested in doing something about them, not graduates of the University of Toronto who have never been outside of this so-called inside lavatory age in which we are living, but people who have had some experience in living in the outside lavatory age in which the Indians are living.
You are hired.

Item agreed to.
Education-
64. Administration, operation and maintenance, $17,734,854.

Mr. Chairman, on this item I would like to do something this evening which nobody appears to have done. I would like to congratulate the minister on the work of her department in education for Indians. I would also like to make just one minor inquiry. In my constituency at the present time a building is almost completed which will contain 166 new classrooms and it is being constructed on the reservation. I still hope the minister will say a little about it. Has it been a success?

We think it has been a success. The only thing that bothers me about these scholarships is that there are not enough of them. I feel very strongly on this and I have said to many people in important places that there is a great deal of latent talent among the Indians. It is not only talent for administration, for teaching, for nursing, but also for the arts. I have already taken some initial steps which I might say involve merely an approach to individuals.
My hope is that in the next couple of years I will be able to encourage young people to come forward and demonstrate their talents in these fields. I may say that we have already taken steps within the department to instruct our teachers throughout Canada to be on the lookout for special skills and talents so that these young people may be encouraged in their early school years to develop the talents they have been given in order that they may have the same opportunities as children in non-Indian schools across Canada to secure scholarships and other assistance which will further their advance in the field of their own particular aptitudes.
I think there was another question I asked the hon. lady about school integration.

Oh yes. While the officials are looking up the actual figures I might just say that progressively each year more and more Indian students attend non-Indian schools, and we think that the further integration of Indian students with non-Indian students is a progressive step, as I know the hon. member also thought when he was the minister of this department. I do not know whether we have any specific figures which I can give. I find that at the present time there are 8,429 Indian students in non-Indian schools out of a total of 38,836 Indian students. In other words, almost 25 per cent of our Indian students are studying in nonIndian schools.
Is that percentage up much from a year ago?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, one of the problems of the department is that once you break a rule you establish a precedent.
I know that very well.
Where there are humanitarian aspects involved I can assure him that in every case I do a great deal of soul searching about the matter.

I am referring only to those cases where young children who are
