I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that even though these children leave the country they are still Canadian children. They are always Canadian children and they are Canadian citizens. They can come back to this country at any time at all. Just how far one goes in condoning the actions of irresponsible parents I do not know. After all, there are people in this country who blight the lives of their children by their own acts. Just how far we go in forgiving parents for their actions because of the fact that they have small children, I do not know. We do not absolve a man from serving his sentence simply because he has children at home. All these things have to be considered. I know the hon. member will realize that I am speaking very much off the cuff without serious consideration of the problem at the moment, but I can assure him that in every one of these cases very serious and soul searching consideration is given.

I should like to say one
more word on the subject. I expressed regret and am very glad to repeat the regret I expressed if in any case I was in fact responsible, as the hon. lady seemed to establish I was-I have not been able to look at the files and I take her word for it-for deporting people who were undoubtedly technically deserving of deportation and thereby exiling Canadian children or causing them to be deserted by their parents. However, I do not think we should do that any longer and, as the hon. lady points out, it is precisely because these children remain Canadian citizens that I think it is all the more important that they should be allowed to grow up in Canada. Whatever the balance of advantage and disadvantage may be, if these children are going to remain Canadian citizens as they are, surely it is more desirable from the point of view of Canada that they should be brought up here in Canada irrespective of what rights there may be in the matter.
As I pointed out, after we established assisted passage loans for dependents, it happened a good many times that we discovered in the department that there were cases of children whose parents had been deported in the 30's because they were on relief, who had been brought up in another country and wanted to come to Canada and could not even get assisted passage loans

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration because, being Canadian citizens, they were not immigrants. Of course, we changed the law and fixed that up.
These cases occur very rarely, as the hon. lady knows. After all, deportation is not a punishment, it is the carrying out of the immigration law. The hon. lady does not conduct trials any more than I did. She reaches an opinion as parliament has asked her to do and deportation should not be regarded as a punishment. It is removing from this country someone whom parliament did not think was desirable as a permanent resident of Canada. I do not question that, on balance, perhaps some of these people are not desirable but if they happen, though undesirable, to be the parents of infant Canadian children who are Canadian citizens it seems to me that the balance should be swung the other way.

In speaking of deportation, I should like to ask the minister whether or not there has been any change in the procedure with respect to telling a person ordered deported the reasons for his deportation.
The deportee knows the reasons for his deportation.

No, the deportee does not know. I have to respectfully differ with the minister. The reasons why he is being deported are not given to the deportee. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister that this is a serious matter and very serious complaints on this subject were made by the present Prime Minister when he sat on this side of the house, and also by the present Minister of Justice. This was one of their basic and most serious charges against the immigration department at that time. They stated that the failure to give reasons to the deportee caused grave injustice.
I should like, for example, to quote the words of the present Minister of Justice as found at page 1158 of Hansard for February 15, 1955. He said:
There is concern and dissatisfaction not only with respect to the over-all policy of the government relative to immigration, which indeed is difficult to determine, but also because of the practices of the government in administering that department, the result of which is to create injustices, hardship, and inequities.
In speaking of a special case he said that the applicant had a right to know the reasons for the refusal to admit his relative. If the minister will permit me-

May I just interrupt here for a moment, if the hon. member will permit. This is precisely the point I was about to make. He is talking about admissions, which
[Mr. Pickersglll.1

is an entirely different thing from deportation. On deportation, it is true that in some cases the evidence is not spelled out completely but the deportee knows under what section of the act he is being deported.

I apologize to the minister. There is a difference between not giving reasons to a deportee and not giving reasons why a relative is not admitted into Canada. Has there been a change in the regulations whereby the department tells the relative in Canada, the Canadian citizen who is bringing someone to Canada, the reasons why the relative is not admitted?

No, there has been no real change yet, although the matter has been under intensive study ever since this government came into power, but it is a most complicated and difficult problem. I believe that in many of these cases the applicant for admission to the country knows the reason for refusal. In some cases, it is possible to tell the sponsor that the applicant knows the reason and if he will ask the applicant for the reason he can tell him. Sometimes the applicant is not willing to divulge to his sponsor what he knows to be the case, and over that we have very little control.

I must again respectfully differ with the minister; that is not the fact as I have learned in some cases. I shall again quote the words of the present Minister of Justice as found at page 7162 of Hansard for August 7, 1956, when he made this very direct statement:
I refer, of course, particularly to the refusal of the department to inform prospective immigrants who are rejected of the reasons for their rejection, which practice is carried over in a number of cases to a refusal to inform people who land in Canada and against whom orders for deportation are made of the reasons for those orders. We have said before and we say again that this practice is absolutely unjustified, that it is contrary to the principles of justice upon which this country's system rests.
That was the position taken by the Minister of Justice at that time. I have similar quotations from the Prime Minister. I agree with the statements made by the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister when they sat in opposition. I want to know if, since they now have the power to remedy these defects which they did not have when they sat in opposition, anything has been done in that direction?

There are two things I should like to say. First of all, in making these remarks when this party was in opposition the present Minister of Justice did admit in this house that he realized it was a very serious and complex problem. When

he came into the government he was Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in addition to being Minister of Justice. One of his first acts was to set up a committee to study this matter.
I dealt with this the other day when we were on citizenship-I do not know if the hon. member was in the house at the time- and I did say with regard to establishing judicial or quasi-judicial boards that the question was still being considered. It has been considered by a cabinet committee for some time now but a definite decision had not yet been reached. I can assure my hon. friend it is a matter of great concern to this government. We are considering it carefully and we hope we will arrive at a solution to the problem. However, I am sure that like the Minister of Justice my hon. friend will agree with me that it is not a problem easy of solution.

I am pleased to hear the hon. lady say that, and she would not expect me to sit here without saying a word about it. While the Minister of Justice did, on one occasion, after I had made a patient explanation, say that it was a difficult problem, no such admission was ever obtained from the Prime Minister, who used far more extreme language about the inhumanity and the brutality of the administration when I was minister. I am very glad to hear the hon. lady say that under the Prime Minister's leadership the same inhumanity and brutality are still being practised.
That I do not concede.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on this item. First of all, I give my support to the words of commendation for the work being done by the national film board, as expressed by the hon. member for Dollard. I am sure there is a growing recognition and understanding of the work which is being done by the national film board and of its value to Canadians generally, particularly in the production of these very excellent documentary films which are making it possible for Canadians to know Canada much better, both its history and geography, and also making it possible for persons living in other countries to know Canada.
As far as my own constituency is concerned, the film councils are increasing in membership and activity, and undertaking more work every year. I must say to the minister that the work of the district representative of the national film board for the Kootenays, whose headquarters is in Nelson, is very much appreciated by the members of the various film councils and also by people living in isolated and small communities for whom the national film board provides an excellent service. I have some very small and isolated communities in my constituency, and the only films and documentaries which they have the opportunity of seeing are those which have been made available by the national film board. I have been asked by a number of organizations, including some of the churches, the Canadian Legion, and some of the women's institutes, to express appreciation of the work being done by the national film board both in the production of these documentary films and also in the work which is being done in the district and the co-operation received from the representative of the board in the Kootenay area.
I cannot sit down without talking very parochially, as one of the pressmen said of me on one occasion. I intend to make some remarks directly related to some propaganda for the area in which I live. There is a great interest in the Columbia and Kootenay regions in the documentary film which it is proposed to make in this area. I hope that when the minister replies to the questions raised by hon. members she will be able to give some fairly accurate and detailed information as to what the board is proposing in this direction, because this documentary film to be made of the Columbia river basin provides the greatest opportunity the board has ever had in Canada. There we have a region of 40,000 square miles
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration with an unusual history and unusually beautiful scenery-mountains, valleys, lakes and rivers. This region has a most interesting history with respect to early navigation, both by the Hudson's Bay Company, later by the stern wheelers, and still later in connection with the lumber and mining operations in the district. The region has a most interesting history with regard to the development of mining, the development of smelting, and the tremendous growth of the forest industry.
Anyone who looks for them will be able to find some particularly interesting small communities-beautiful small communities located on the Kootenay and Arrow lakes as well as on various parts of the Columbia and Kootenay rivers. These communities would provide charming opportunities for producers of the national film board. I hope, too, that when the producers of the board-those who plan these things-are arranging the content of this film they will consult with the provincial organizations-the British Columbia historical association, to name one-and with the local historical societies. I also suggest that if they wish to get a little colour into the film they should consult with a few people of ancient vintage who live in the Columbia basin and thus get in touch with those fast disappearing "characters" who are required to make any film particularly memorable and striking.
I must repeat that the people of our district are looking forward to the production of this film. All the local organizations are willing to co-operate in any way they can in what, I have no doubt, will turn out to be the greatest and most successful venture ever undertaken by the board in the realm of documentary films in this area.

The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me about the United Nations film. As the hon. gentleman knows, this film was made by the national film board for the United Nations as a joint venture. As a matter of fact I believe the United Nations was about to send their own people into the field when they realized that the national film board was already on the scene and so they commissioned the film board to make the film. It is in the custody of the United Nations as regards its distribution. I have no information other than that. It has not been released to date and permission has not been procured for its release.

Would the hon. lady tell us how much the film cost the Canadian taxpayer, if anything, and whether or not any recent efforts have been made to secure the film from the United Nations for distribution in Canada? As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I do not think we are in a position to run counter to the wishes of the United Nations with regard to the release of the film. I am not in a position to answer for the Department of External Affairs and I believe that question might more properly be asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Certainly we are in no position to distribute the film independently of the wishes of the United Nations in that regard.

May I pursue that a little further. Could the hon. lady say if permission was sought and refused at the United Nations or if no steps have been taken in the matter. It seems a rather odd thing that a film made by the national film board of Canada would be censored by the U.N. Since this was one of the undertakings of the film board surely it is something of which we ought to have an account.

That might appear to be so. The cost of the film which was assumed by the film board for its activities was $42,460.71. That is not the total cost because some of it was borne by the United Nations. If the Leader of the Opposition will permit me, I have a short statement I would like to make with reference to the national gallery.
It has been known since the spring of 1955 that the national gallery would move to the Lome building some time during 1959. It is now confirmed that the move will take place on or about September 30.
The move to the new building will have a number of important results in terms of services to the public, both Canadian and tourist. All of the important works in the collection will be on public view; there will be space, at last, to show and properly to house the print and drawing collection, which is one of the finest in terms of quality in North America; there will be sufficient room to show a reasonable proportion of the war collections; all the important works in the sculpture collection, which is a small one, will be on view. We will have our own auditorium and we will be able to present a greatly increased and far more systematic program of public lectures, film programs, and so forth. There will be sufficient space for the scientific and conservation laboratory to develop and expand into a truly national service; the design centre will return to its old site at the corner of Albert and Slater; the library and photographic library service will have sufficient space for these services to operate at a level worthy of a national gallery; the workshop area in the double basement will allow the extension and travelling exhibition services to operate with proper efficiency. Perhaps the greatest gain of all is that special exhibitions can be mounted without displacing the permanent collection.
The prospect of the move to a new building has affected the work and program of the gallery profoundly over the past four years. The staff has been slowly increased- it is now almost double what it was in 1955- as people could be found and trained for both the increased curatorial work which will result from a much greater proportion of the national collection being on public view and also to deal with a greatly expanded extension program serving some 120 centres across the country.

Mr. Chairman, the committee, I think, will have learned with satisfaction of the progress made in the transfer of the gallery to its new building, a project which was initiated, as the minister knows, some few years ago before she was so happily in charge of the department.
While I congratulate the minister on that progress report, I am afraid I cannot congratulate her in regard to a matter which I wish to bring up at this time, undoubtedly not to her surprise, and which is concerned with the possible purchase or negotiations for the purchase of a picture for the gallery, a Breughel.
I think I should begin by pointing out to the committee that I believe the minister was not in charge of the department after the change of government when negotiations for the purchase of this picture began, and therefore she does not have any direct responsibility perhaps for the sorry, unhappy ending of these negotiations. I have had the opportunity of making some investigation into this matter and, as I have just said, it is a confused, unhappy situation which brings no credit to the government and which, on the contrary, has resulted in a good deal of discredit to the government and to the name of Canada in those circles which are concerned with art matters.
What I am dealing with is not the desirability or otherwise of spending a large sum of money at this time for the purchase of a picture, however rare and beautiful that picture may be. The question at issue is the way in which this matter was handled or rather mishandled, as I see it, by the government. The reply by the minister, to be found on page 1364 of Hansard for February 25, to a question put on the order paper by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate concerning this matter certainly does not mitigate the complaint that we have to make with regard to the way the matter was dealt with.
If I am inaccurate in giving my account of these negotiations no doubt the minister, who has the records at her disposal, will correct me. As I understand the situation, the first contact between a representative of the gallery and the agent for the owner of the picture, a landscape by Breughel, was made on January 4, 1957, when the gallery became interested in what perhaps is one of the finest pictures of its kind in the world and one of the very few pictures of this artistic value which was open for purchase. I believe that in January of 1957 a value of approximately $500,000 was placed on the picture by the European owner.
A good many months later, on October 22, 1957, after the election of that year, I believe
1904	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the owner of the picture or the agent of the owner was informed that the trustees of the national gallery, who would naturally have to pass on any purchase of a picture of this kind or any other kind, were interested and I believe the director was authorized at that time to pursue the matter further and no doubt report back. I am informed that in October of 1957 the amount involved was far beyond the appropriation of the national gallery.
However, in December, 1957, the officers of the gallery, no doubt with authority, pursued the question of price with the owner or the agent of the owner of the picture. I am informed that in January, 1958 the agent for the owner of the picture was told that the trustees of the national gallery of Canada had unanimously expressed the intention to acquire this painting if negotiations could be satisfactorily concluded, that negotiations then began with the owner or agent on the question of price and that late in January, 1958 the owner was then informed that there would be a delay because of the political situation in Canada and the approach of an election and nothing could be worked out very quickly on that account.
But in February the agent did learn that the trustees were pursuing the matter of the purchase and that question was before the government at that time for a definite opinion on whether or not the picture should be bought. Then, toward the end of April the owner or agent was informed that the trustees of the national gallery had agreed on a figure which, if other aspects of the matter could be cleared up, might be offered to the owner, that figure being $350,000, well below the amount I have quoted as being the value placed on the picture some time earlier by the owner. It was considerably less than that earlier value.
I have already referred to the answer given by the minister to the question asked in the house. As found on page 1364 of Hansard the minister made this reply:
-the board of trustees of the national gallery had asked-
Presumably had asked the government.
-for "authorization to negotiate for the purchase of the Breughel owned by Baron von Polnitz". At the same time the trustees asserted that the necessary funds had been appropriated and were available for the purchase. This statement was confirmed by the director of the gallery.
I gather from that that the government got their information as to the availability of funds for this picture not from any treasury board authority, not from the Department of Finance but from the officers of the national gallery, from the director and trustees of the national gallery. Having received their


information not from treasury board but from the trustees and the director of the national gallery, according to the answer to this question, that money was available, on the basis of that information the cabinet on May 2 authorized the Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to give permission to the director to proceed accordingly. Apparently, by that it meant to proceed with the negotiations for the purchase of the picture.
I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that on the other end of the deal a very different understanding prevailed. I am informed that the agent for the owner was told by the director of the gallery that he was authorized, not merely to negotiate as stated in the answer to this question but to make an offer of $350,000 for this picture, presumably on the understanding that this money was available, on the basis of information secured from the gallery itself and not from the treasury board or the Department of Finance or the other authorities of government which might be expected to know.
He was authorized to make an offer, authorized by the government to make an offer of this amount without any strings attached, with payment to be made on delivery of the picture sometime after May 12. The agent was asked, as a matter of urgency, to get a reply from the owner. He got in touch with the owner on May 3 and the owner assumed that this was an offer made in good faith, a valid offer, without any strings attached. The owner accepted the offer and the agent wired the director of the gallery accordingly and requested, I am informed, written confirmation.
Then on May 5 the director of the gallery told the agent that he would send a purchase contract in a few days and payment would be made. There would be a little delay in making payment because it would have to wait until after parliament convened, but that would be a mere formality. Then three days later the director, after all these negotiations had been completed, informed the agent that there would be difficulty in regard to the financing of this picture because the cabinet had authorized this firm offer on the understanding that the money was readily available from some fund which was in existence for the purchase of pictures from the Liechtenstein collection. Now they discovered, after this firm offer had been made, that there was no such money readily available from that fund. The agent was informed that it was hoped this difficulty would soon be cleared up and the contract could be signed.

It was not until four or five days after that, on May 12 or May 13, that finally the agent for the owner of this picture was able to see the minister concerned, and the minister then explained that this was all very unfortunate; that there had been a misunderstanding; that the money which was thought to be available was not available and therefore the deal, if I may put it this way, was off and no purchase would be made.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that, according to my information, is an account of the events leading up to the decision of the government, first to authorize the firm offer and eventually to withdraw that firm offer and tell the owner of the picture that the deal was off. Perhaps in the present circumstances it was a very wise decision not to spend the money for the picture at this time-I am not qualified to judge-but surely, the way this was done reflects no credit on anybody concerned with it. I am sure it has given Canada a very bad name in circles which deal in art matters. Perhaps this may not be of any immediate importance to Canadians but it will do Canada no good in future when we wish to add valuable pictures to our national gallery.
Perhaps I could complete this sorry record of mishandling by asking the minister, who would no doubt wish to reply to what I have said, whether at any time the owner has, since this date I have mentioned of May 13, asked for an interview with the Prime Minister or any minister to get an explanation why this matter was handled in this way? Has the minister any other information she could give to us about this matter which, as I have already said and I repeat, was an unfortunate example of confusion, fumbling, bumbling and mishandling.

May I preface my remarks by saying I have no apology to make for the action of the government with regard to this particular matter. The Leader of the Opposition has seen fit to read into the record his own assumptions with respect to what might have taken place in the negotiations for the purchase of the Breughel. I made my statement in the house, as he has said, on February 25, after due consideration. I should like to quote the last two paragraphs of that statement in which I said:
It is clear that no authority existed to make a firm offer or enter into a contract for this purchase by the national gallery or the government of Canada or anyone on its or their behalf. The Financial Administration Act specifically requires that there be an appropriation provided by parliament for the purpose before a contract can be made.
It is reiterated that the authority asked for was to negotiate. Although granted in the first instance this was immediately revoked as soon as the lack of appropriation was revealed.
Business of the House
The Leader of the Opposition has been at some pains to castigate the government for its lack of knowledge of what funds had been appropriated. But the Leader of the Opposition has been a minister of the crown as well as a deputy minister, and I think he knows that the minister relies upon information which is given to him by his officials.
I also know that the minister takes responsibility for all acts of his officials.

That is all well and good; then, is the Leader of the Opposition suggesting to me now that he is castigating the government or is he casting reflections upon the director of the national gallery or upon the board of trustees?

I will answer that question. I am casting reflections upon the government which must take the responsibility for the way these negotiations were conducted. Perhaps the minister, if she thinks my information is wrong, will table all the correspondence in connection with this matter, all the letters, telegrams, records of telephone calls and any material which will throw any light on this situation?

If the Leader of the Opposition wishes to request in specific terms what he requires to be tabled we will be glad to look into it. I would say to him that because of his long experience in government, both as a civil servant and as a minister of the crown, he knows very well that the government has no power to spend funds which have not been appropriated.
They should find that out.
The minister should know that before making any commitments.

There was no appropriation and, as the Leader of the Opposition stated, this did not happen during my term of office. I will say that I would not condone the expenditure of funds and I would not ask parliament to provide funds to cover up a fiasco like this.

subsubtopic: QUALIFICATIONS OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
What qualities and qualifications are desirable in a director of: (a) the human history branch of the national museum of Canada; (b) the natural history branch of the national museum of Canada?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilion (Minister of
Northern Affairs and National Resources):
(a) and (b). In addition to good health and personal suitability, the desirable qualities in a director of either branch of the national museum of Canada comprise a sound knowledge of and capacity for management and administration, organizational ability, and capacity to co-ordinate research. Specific qualifications include:	graduation with a
doctor's degree from a university of recognized standing with specialization in one or more of the related fields; extensive experience in one or more of the disciplines involved and an international standing as shown by published results; experience in planning, exhibits and a knowledge of modern museum and public information methods. In the case of a director of the human history branch, it might be expected to find a candidate with specialization and experience in fields or disciplines such as anthropology, ethnology or archaeology. In the case of a director of the natural history branch it might be expected to find a candidate with specialization and experience in fields or disciplines such as geology, minerology, palaeontology, zoology or botany.

subsubtopic: STRONTIUM
speechtext:
1.	Is the Minister of National Health and Welfare in a position to comment on a newspaper article appearing in the Financial Post, February 28, 1959, alleging that the existing federal radioactivity-testing program is inadequate?
2.	Will the minister give assurance regarding the safety of milk from excessive doses of strontium 90?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monleilh (Minister
of National Health and Welfare):
1.	The best evidence available shows that the existing Canadian radioactivity testing program compares most favourably with those of other leading countries in the nuclear field. A study of the report of the United Nations scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation of August, 1958, confirms this view. Since the beginning of this program in 1955, the Department of National Health and Welfare has built a new radiochemical building in Ottawa, the number of scientific and technical positions has been substantially increased and at this very moment the department is broadening the scope of its investigations to include measurements of radioactivity in rainfall, air and soil. The program is further supported by the recent construction of two whole-body measuring units for the determination of radioactivity in humans. The department has planned to build a third Canadian unit of this type which it considers an essential part of the studies.
The department is keeping abreast of all new scientific developments in this field and to this end the program is kept under constant review.
2.	Excessive levels of strontium 90 have occurred only on nuclear weapon testing sites, of which there is none in Canada. On the basis of findings of the Department of National Health and Welfare there is at present no discernible hazard by strontium 90 contamination of milk.

What is the explanation of the substantial differences between: (a) the principal amount of the conversion loan bonds as given in the January 1959 Bank of Canada statistical summary; (b) the principal amount for the same loans given in the December 1958 Bank of Canada statistical summary?
Answer by: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
The principal amounts of conversion loan bonds given in the December 1958 statistical summary of the Bank of Canada and labelled "preliminary" were the same as those given in the Department of Finance press release of October 21, 1958, covering statistics as of October 14, 1958. The figures were estimates based on reports received directly from authorized agents during the campaign and in the press release were footnoted as "subject to revision on completion of final accounting by issuing agents," The figures in the January statistical summary are based on a near final accounting by issuing agents. Minor adjustments may still be made and the figures are still labelled "preliminary".
